en: The Heart Sutra of the Great Perfection of Wisdom Commentary by the Daoist of Songxi,
Wugouzi (The Stainless One) This point of numinous light ascends upon the Way;
It is only because of chasing after delusions that one falls into the dust.
If you now wish to see the road back to your native land, awaken to the Heart Sūtra and the Eye of the Way shall open—*Mahā*.
This is a Sanskrit term from the Western Heavens; translated into the language of this Eastern Land, it means "Great. Furthermore, "Great" refers to that which is vast and without boundary.
That which is vast and boundless is none other than the Great Way of empty space. Master Chuan said: "The realm of empty space cannot be conceived;
the principle of the Great Way is pure, secluded, and even more expansive. He also said: "In the ten directions there are no walls, and on the eight sides there are no gates;
the Great Way has no boundaries, and empty space is difficult to measure. Thus it is called the Way.

"Meeting it, one does not see its head; following it, one does not see its rear. The Confucians say: "The higher one looks up at it, the higher it rises; the deeper one drills into it, the harder it proves.
Looking for it, it seems to be in front; suddenly it is behind. All the sages and saints have praised it in this way as something vast and great.
Although the sun and moon are bright, their light cannot compare to its radiance; although heaven and earth are vast, they cannot match its magnitude.
It encompasses all forms and can give birth to the myriad phenomena, yet its shape is not seen; it pervades the sands of all worlds, yet no trace of it is observed.
Although it is thus vast and profound, who knows that there is yet another thing that surpasses this?
Tell me, what is it? Do you recognize this circle (○)? When wide, it contains the entire Dharma-realm; when narrow—
Thus, when manifest, not even a hair’s breadth remains unpenetrated, reaching everywhere throughout the eight wildernesses and nine barbarian tribes;
when hidden, it enters even the finest specks and subtle dust. Now, without avoiding even a hundred million transgressions, this clearly revealed and leaked [truth] is the very source of humanity.
As the Immortal Master said: "Why does this mind open the Great Way? It is simply because from the beginning it was directed toward it."

Coming from along the Way: that people of the world cannot return to their origin is because they mistakenly identify the physical body as themselves, being deceived by the six sense organs and obscured by the seven emotions;
thus, they lose their own true nature and wander through birth and death. Do you wish to see this true nature?
You will not find it by searching, nor will you find it by seeking; it is right here, circling within the twelve hours of the day.
The body turns—do you realize this?
The Dharma-body is like the vast void; the nature of the Way has always been one and the same.
It is only because of chasing after delusions and losing sight of true nature that one wanders through the cycle of the six realms.
*Prajñā* is a term from the Sanskrit language of the Western Heavens; in the Eastern Land, it is translated as "wisdom" (*hui-zhi*).
Furthermore, wisdom refers to correct knowledge, correct understanding, and discernment. A practitioner of the Way must employ the power of wisdom to subdue the body and mind.
One must not allow oneself to be unrestrained in order to practice tranquil concentration (*śamatha-vipaśyanā*).

The Way says: "One is able to subdue all demons and spirits through the power of wisdom. The Lotus Sūtra says: "The sun of wisdom destroys all darkness and can subdue calamitous winds and fires. Confucianism says:
"Wisdom (*zhi*) can destroy the heterodox, while insight (*hui*) can destroy darkness. Furthermore, ignorant and foolish people perform their deeds with coarseness and evil.

I am unwilling to engage in the threefold reflection, but instead strive for extensive learning and vast erudition; my thoughts are set on boastful talk and debate rather than investigating the life-and-death matter of my own house.
I delight in seeking out the faults of others and fail to draw near to those who are true practitioners of the Way.

I prefer the company of superficial Chan adepts who engage in empty talk about the scriptures of the sages, yet apply no effort whatsoever to the cultivation of their own minds. I plot for fame and crave profit.
Those who are arrogant and conceited speak only of the light of the present moment and do not contemplate what lies behind them;
such people are clever heretics. As an ancient worthy said: "Heretics may be clever, but they lack true wisdom."
The Immortal Master said: "To speak with the mouth while failing to practice with the mind is not the mark of a refined person. The Confucian says:
"First govern the self and the body, and afterwards govern the family, the state, and the world. Furthermore, a person of wisdom acts with composure and deliberation, refusing to act impulsively;
they recognize cause and effect, regard sin and merit, draw near to those of knowledge, inquire of the perfected ones, and exhaustively investigate the nature of life.
Investigating the root source of the great matter of birth and death, one subdues body and mind and gathers in the spirit and vital energy.

With every thought dwelling in the Way and every breath returning to the Truth, when the day comes that merit is perfected and practice is fulfilled, with a single "thump" of the earth, one breaks through the three realms.
This void merges into a single essence; once this stage is reached, neither the transformations of creation nor the interplay of Yin and Yang can alter it.
The four seasons cannot mold him; the five elements cannot shift him; spirits and ghosts cannot employ him; even the kalpa-ending conflagration cannot destroy him.
He has become a carefree and autonomous being, an idle man beyond the mundane world. Do you wish to see this idle man beyond the mundane world?
Though he constantly enters and exits through the six gates, although he is near, he is not intimate.
With eyes wide open, do not let the opportunity slip away—do you understand?
The paths of wisdom and cleverness diverge; cleverness is but the branches and leaves, while wisdom is the root and sprout.
If one transforms ignorance into wisdom, the withered tree of many years will bloom of its own accord.
*Pāra*. "Pāra" is a Sanskrit term from the Western Heavens; in the Eastern Land, it is translated as "the other shore. This shore refers to the boundary of birth and death;
the other shore refers to the shore beyond birth and death. Those who are deluded are on this shore; those who have attained awakening are on the other shore. The world [is thus divided].

If a person is deluded regarding their original nature, they are ignorant and inverted; they identify the four elements and six sense organs as themselves, contending for fame and competing for profit.

They scheme for a livelihood lasting a thousand years and accumulate grievances and karmic debts spanning ten thousand kalpas. Turning their backs on awakening and uniting with the dust of the world, they lose the true and pursue the false, busily rushing about without knowing when to rest.
Moment by moment, the dualities of mind and environment remain unremoved. Suddenly, one morning—
When the great limit arrives and one departs, there are no means to act; here one strips off the damp cloth shirt, and there one puts on the lice-infested tunic.
Going and coming, changing one’s appearance, like ants circling in a loop, when will it ever end?
In this sea of suffering of birth and death, when will one find the crossing? Those who act in such a manner remain only on this shore.

There is a person who suddenly awakens to the realization that all they have previously done and created is entirely false; they cast aside the false to follow the true, exhausting the roots and investigating the source.
They constantly draw near to the sages and always associate with spiritual friends, seeking the boat for reaching the other shore and finding the oar of skillful means.
Thus they cross over the river of craving and the sea of suffering to ascend to the other shore, attaining liberation from the great flood of birth and death.
Pō no longer drags along mud or water; he is a man of dry feet and clean hands, pure, free, and at ease.
But tell me, how does one reach the other shore? Heh! It is difficult for others to exert effort;
one must cross over one’s own body by oneself. Do you understand?
Wisdom is the boat, diligence the oar; exerting strength at the spiritual citadel, one emerges from the waves and turns back to ascend directly to the shore of Bodhi.
Casting off all attachments, one returns to where the bright moon is high—this is Prajñāpāramitā.
The term from the Western Heaven (India) is *Brahman*; in the Eastern Land, it is translated as "Wuji" (Ultimatelessness). Furthermore, "mi" means harmony, and "he" means a great gathering.
Moreover, "Wuji" refers to that which is supremely high and supremely great, such that it is difficult to reach its limit.

The Buddhists call it *Wuji* (Ultimatelessness); the Daoists call it *Taiji* (Supreme Ultimate); and the Confucians call it *Huangji* (August Ultimate)—all refer to this very same reality. Now, this is clearly evident.
To say that even a single word of the "Opening of the Secret" (*kaimi*) exceeds the Great Way (*daodao*) and empty space (*kūkyō*) refers to the myriad phenomena (*man'e*).
This is because the Way is able to contain all categories of existence; whether sentient or insentient, they are all entirely within the Great Way.

Human true nature (*shinsei*) is likewise identical in this regard, for it can also encompass all dharmas (*banpō*), and all dharmas are entirely contained within this single nature. Thus, it is vast.
Within the void there are eighty-four thousand diverse natures that cannot be fully described; they all reside within the single nature of humanity.
This single nature is like honey, and these natures are likened to the various flavors.
Because the practitioner harmonizes these diverse natures with this single nature and unites them into one, it is called *madhya* (honey). The Way says: "Recognize it."
"Ten thousand matters are finished. The Buddhist says: "The myriad dharmas return to the One.
The Confucian says: "My Way is unified by the One. But tell me, what is this One? Do you recognize this circle (○)?
*Dot!* Where the five elements do not reach, before the parents were yet born— Though it may be explained, it cannot be practiced; it is difficult.
Upon arrival, you must go directly to exhaust all defilements before you can see [it].
Do you understand? The single nature is the honey; the many are the bees. First, take the awakened nature and blend it universally and evenly.
Sitting, it becomes a single piece of true suchness-nature. The single nature, perfectly luminous, ascends to the Great Terrace.
The Mind.
The mind is the fundamental source of humanity. All phenomena, without exception, are entirely contained within this single mind.
There are eighty-four thousand [afflictions], which are infinite and inexhaustible when in motion, yet remain unchanging and immovable when in stillness. The commentary states:
"When the mind arises, all phenomena arise; when the mind ceases, all phenomena cease. The Daoists say:
"When the mind dies, the moon of one's nature shines with clarity; when the mind arises, the dust of desire obscures it. The Confucians say: "If one restrains the single mind, there is stillness;
if one plots amidst many affairs, there is chaos. Therefore, the ancient sages taught their disciples to withdraw and collect their minds back into themselves.
In one place it is called "The Ten Thousand Dharmas Return to One," and in another it is named the "Dharma Gate of the Single Syllable.
Because people do not believe that the mind is Buddha and that the mind creates Buddha, various skillful means are employed to point out to the world so that they may see their own original nature.
Have you not seen the ancients say: "The three dots are like the stars; the horizontal hook resembles the slanting moon"?
That Māo attained Buddhahood from this is precisely because of this: ascending to heaven and entering the earth are both accomplished by what one does within one's own mind;
they are not obtained elsewhere. As the Sūtra says: "Dwelling in a secluded place, collect and restrain the mind."
It is further said: "If one can control [the mind] in a single place, there is no task that cannot be accomplished.

Those who are unable to return to this oneness do so because those who recognize the mind are few while those whose nature is distracted are many; thus they lose the True Way. Why is it that they do not recognize their own minds? It is because they are beset by many delusions;

their natures are all impaired as they lose their spirit and fall into obscurity, chasing after external objects and losing their minds. Their six sense organs are internally blind, and they remain attached to material things."
The nature of disorder does not give rise to wisdom because of the darkness of ignorance. If you are willing to cultivate the mind, exhaust the mysteries of life and destiny,
investigate birth and death, draw near to an enlightened master, and seek the medicinal Dharma to treat the maladies of the heart—

keeping this in mind at all times, walking step by step, never forgetting it while sitting or lying down, and remaining inseparable from this very circle (○) whether speaking or silent, moving or still— suddenly, between the eyebrows...
The hair stands on end and the eyes are opened wide, revealing one’s original face. But tell me, what is the shape of this original face?
An old master of Chuanshou said: "Fire cannot burn it, water cannot drown it, wind cannot blow it away, and a blade cannot cleave it.
It is as soft as *tūla* cotton, yet as hard as an iron wall; it exists throughout heaven and earth."
Ancients and moderns alike fail to recognize it—*tut*! Do you know it? Constantly facing it all day long, you do not know who this person is.
This wheel of the mind-mirror is originally free of dust; because of dust, it is difficult to reflect one's original truth.
When dust is cleared and the mirror is bright, there is not a single thing; the body of the Dharma King naturally manifests.
"Sūtra" (ching) means "path" (ching); it is the path upon which worldly people cultivate their practice. When a student attains this, they have no doubt.
If you intend to rest, do not let the project go astray; proceed directly, and there will surely come a time when you reach home.
I only fear that the path may not be true, leading you to walk in error and mistake your way. Tell me, where are you going? I shall now speak clearly:
it is toward a place where not even an inch of grass grows, where not a speck of dust stands, and which is pure, free from mud and water, and devoid of pits or hollows.
Naked, bare, and stark, in a state of perfect stability, one suddenly encounters a perfectly round, brilliantly shining, eternally indestructible wish-fulfilling jewel of radiant light.
Taking it up with one's own hands, one attains great utility and is no longer subject to suffering.
The commentary says: "The *maṇi* jewel. The Path says: "The *śyāmāka* grain."
The Mysterious Pearl: The Confucians call it the "nine-bend bright pearl. Do you wish to see this pearl? Seek it with single-mindedness beyond the realm of forms;
do not seek it within the mundane world.
This true sūtra is originally within the mind; The treasure hidden in one's own house need not be sought.
Suddenly encountering the Chapter on Non-arising, A bright pearl bursts forth, illuminating past and present—Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva.
The state of mastery possessed by Bodhisattvas exists within every person; it is only because of the obstructions created by the six sense organs and their objects that one is unable to perceive it.
Being pulled by the myriad conditions of emotional desire, one fails to attain mastery.
If there is a person of wisdom who can believe in this and let go, simply settling the body and mind in a secluded and quiet place, sitting until they are utterly still and tranquil—this is mastery.
In the midst of profound stillness, without even a hair’s breadth of divergent thought, the single mind is pure and maintains the ultimate state of quiescence.
Suddenly, with a start, there is a True Person within one's own spiritual palace, coming and going, moving freely and without obstruction.
Only here does one see oneself as a Bodhisattva, perfect and sovereign; in a single kṣaṇa, one pervades the entire realm of saṃsāra.
The Dharma-body manifests everywhere, yet leaves no trace wherever it goes; its radiance shines universally, and though one contemplates it, it cannot be seen.
If people wish to see this Bodhisattva, they need not use their eyes to look, nor their ears to listen.
Only by relinquishing the functions of the eyes and ears can one recognize the sovereign Bodhisattva. As the Way says: "I cannot be seen by looking, nor heard by listening."
To not hear and to be free from all extremes is called the Sublime Way. The *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* says:
"If one sees me by means of form, or seeks me by means of sound, such a person walks a deviant path and cannot see the Tathāgata.
The Confucians say: "Seeing without using the eyes and hearing without using the ears—to transcend the functions of the eyes and ears, one naturally attains the nature."
Only those such as these truly know that this true immortal Bodhisattva has never been absent—sitting together, walking together, sharing joy, and sharing laughter;
not a single step has they ever been apart. It is only that you yourself have remained oblivious.
Do you wish to see this Bodhisattva? Aha! Although their coming and going leave no trace, they shine forth brilliantly.
Do you see this radiance?
The Bodhisattva has never been apart from the body; it is only that you yourself have been oblivious and failed to recognize it.
If you can sit in stillness and reflect the light back upon yourself, you will immediately see the original master of your former life.

Practice. "Practice" refers to the cultivation of conduct. When paths are rugged and unrefined, they are difficult to traverse; yet one must cultivate them. This cultivation is the training of the mind toward the Way;
this practice is the performance of goodness that leads back to True Suchness (*tathatā*). It is similar to a person repairing a road by clearing away the thorns and brambles obstructing the path.
Clear away the stubborn rocks of the path: those that are high, cut them down; those that are low, fill them up.
Sweep and cleanse until it is level and smooth. One’s own mind-ground must also be cultivated in this way:
exert effort to eliminate all thoughts of harming others for one's own benefit, just as one removes thorns obstructing the road to ensure a steady and secure journey. Eliminate everything.
The causes and conditions by which discursive thoughts obstruct the Path are like stubborn rocks in the way; one must remove them so that the body may advance upon a level and upright path.

To diminish great excesses and supplement deficiencies so as to achieve equilibrium, to clear away the defiled mind and sever all taints, and to strike it down until it is pure—this is the essential point for entering the gate of cultivation at its very beginning.
It is not a matter of mere words, nor is it merely a matter of physical action.
"It relies entirely on cultivating the ground of the mind. The Immortals and Sages say that cultivating the ground of the mind means completely casting aside worldly affairs.

The Buddhists say that the Dharma-gate of the ground of the mind does not reside in verbal eloquence. The Confucians say that speaking is not as good as practicing, and practicing is not as good as reaching this state.
Furthermore, one must observe from where this step arises; if one knows its point of origin, then...

Knowing the Source of Birth and Death: In the past, Liu Haiyue visited Master Baiyun and, after prostrating, asked: "Disciple, my discursive thoughts cannot be subdued; what should I do? The Master asked: "Who is it that has these discursive thoughts? He replied: "Disciple. The Master said: "Who is it that subdues them? Haiyue seemed to have an inkling of understanding yet lacked full realization; he pondered with a faint smile. The Master [said]: "Discourse on the Source of Birth and Death" By Master Baiyun Shouduan The nature of the mind is originally empty and still;

Birth and death are but delusive appearances. If you can recognize the source of birth and death, Then you will see that there is no self at all. Liu Haiyue once visited Master Baiyun and, after prostrating, asked: "Disciple, my discursive thoughts cannot be subdued; what should I do? The Master asked: "Who is it that has these discursive thoughts? He replied: "Disciple. The Master said: "Who is it that subdues them? Haiyue seemed to have an inkling of understanding yet lacked full realization; he pondered with a faint smile. The Master [said]:

"The mind is originally empty and still; Birth and death are but delusive appearances. If you can recognize the source of birth and death, Then you will see that there is no self at all. At that moment, Haiyue attained great enlightenment. He subsequently composed this verse: "The nature of the mind is originally empty and still; Birth and death are but delusive appearances. If you can recognize the source of birth and death, Then you will see that there is no self at all. The Master praised him, saying: "Excellent! You have truly seen your original face. (Note: The final line of the verse and the concluding narrative are provided as part of the traditional record of this encounter.)
"Clouds coming and going are entirely due to you; how chaotic it is! You have no mastery. If you cannot overcome him, then let go.
But you must further know who it is that lets go. If you recognize this, you will naturally possess mastery and will not be deceived by him.
Haichue subsequently attained realization and merely bowed in gratitude. Furthermore, regarding Master Shishuang:
Question: "When Master Shitou says that 'a thought arises and does not stop,' what is this? Shitou rebuked him, saying: "Who is it that gives rise to the thought?
At these words, Shishuang attained great enlightenment. One should simply investigate in this manner, moment after moment, never departing from the present state.
Observe with subtle discernment from where thoughts, deliberations, speech, and perceptions arise. — Ancient Record
It is said: "If you wish to know where the Buddha has gone, it is precisely these very words. The Master said:

"If you wish to know the fundamental source of one's original nature, it is not apart from speech, movement, and stillness. Master Baogong said: "For those who have not yet attained realization, listen to this one word:
who is it that is moving their mouth right now? Although he speaks thus, there is an even more wondrous place beyond what has been explained.
If one practices without acting, one cannot arrive on one's own; yet if the fruit of practice reaches one’s hometown, then the journey is at an end.
Furthermore, as for the distance to one’s hometown: if one is deluded, ten thousand mountains and rivers stand between;
if one awakens, turning one’s head back is home itself. Do you understand this principle?
At first, recognize the truth of the teachings through practice; If you lose your footing, you will forfeit your very life.
When you have firmly established yourself upon the land of your native home, You become a person of carefree and spontaneous ease. Deep.
The "profound" refers to that which is obscure, subtle, and wondrous, penetrating to the very bone and marrow.
To reach such a state, one must first clear away all burdens and become light and agile. The Daoist says: "Diminish it again and again until one reaches non-action (*wuwei*).
The Buddhist says: "Relinquish, and relinquish again; naturally, body and mind will become light and agile. The Confucian says: "If one is truly..."
"Renew yourself daily; renew yourself day after day; renew yourself again and again.

To achieve this, one must practice *zazen* (seated meditation), sweeping away [delusions] day and night until there is nothing left to sweep, until one is as naked as a babe before birth, as if having been cremated.
As the ancients said: "Strip off even the undergarment clinging to the skin, and seek within yourself until all is vast and open."
There is no natural way to reach home; tell me, why is it that one cannot return?
Aha! The day is late and the journey long; the body is weary and the burden heavy. Do you realize this?
The Great Way’s homeland is fundamentally not deep; Worldly people carry heavy burdens and thus find it hard to seek.
If one can let go and become entirely free of things, One will immediately see the Buddha-mind of the Vulture Peak: Prajñā.
*Prajñā* is a Sanskrit term from the Western Heavens; in the Eastern Land, it is translated as "wisdom.

Generally speaking, to be a human being, one must necessarily generate wisdom within oneself. If one lacks wisdom, one is truly a fool who has lived a life in vain, willingly submitting to the gate of death.
There is a certain class of people lacking wisdom who mistake mere cleverness for wisdom; this is a great error.
Furthermore, those who are clever and discerning display their acumen and exhaust their mental faculties;

their speech is as swift as a soaring dragon or a sharp falcon, yet their conduct is like that of a lame tortoise or a sick turtle. Greedy for profit and intent on fame, they treat the coarse as if it were subtle.
They view worldly wealth as mere bone or marrow, while they discard their own lives and natures as if they were excrement or soil, caring only for tomorrow and the day after.

Year after year, one does not realize that old age is approaching; when the limit of death arrives at one's head, it is regrettable to have let time pass in vain and to have labored for a lifetime in such a manner.
If one acts in this way, how can one escape the cycle of birth and death?

A person of wisdom appears outwardly like a fool, yet inwardly remains silent and composed; they recognize that there is birth and death, and they awaken to the fact that there is nothing to be attained.
Without ever losing this constancy, one should personally and truthfully contemplate: from where does birth come, and to where does death go?
Giving rise to this single thought, one should draw near to those of wisdom and consult the perfected ones, seeking the Dharma that transcends the world and the path for escaping birth and death.

One should avoid transgressions and evils as one avoids needles and knives, and cherish one’s life and nature as one cherishes precious gems. In every movement, one should bring peace to others and benefit all beings.
Furthermore, one is not deceived by external objects; when still, one enters meditative concentration (*samādhi*) to contemplate emptiness, no longer lingering in the state of wild wandering.
For such a person, once the fruit is perfected, they wave their hands and return home, attaining great mastery. As the former Master said:

"One day, having attained the return to one's hometown, one is no longer a drifting guest. The Commentary says: "Having cast off the hand upon arrival at home, people do not recognize [him]; furthermore..."
Not a single thing is offered to the honored hall. An old man of the river says: "The lone boat reaches the shore;
the far traveler returns home. Now tell me, what is this "home"? *Pah!* Far away, it is ten thousand eight thousand miles;
near at hand, it does not depart from its current place. Do you understand?
Wisdom and intelligence always reside within the mind; the wise cultivate the internal while the ignorant seek outwardly.
If one possesses wisdom that transcends the three realms, the foolish person lacking wisdom stands on the brink of birth and death.
*Pāramitā*.
*Pāra* is a Sanskrit term from the Western Heavens; in the Eastern Land, it is translated as "reaching the other shore.

Furthermore, those who are deluded undergo birth and death and fall into the cycle of *saṃsāra*, remaining only on this shore. Those who have attained awakening transcend birth and death and escape the cycle of *saṃsāra*, reaching the other shore.
If one wishes to reach the other shore, one must personally generate wisdom to cross over this birth and death.

The ocean of suffering is like a person crossing water; because the depth is difficult to traverse, one must employ various expedients such as boats, bridges, wooden planks, or bamboo rafts to carry oneself across this ocean of suffering and reach the other shore.

Once the other shore has been reached, the aforementioned boats, bridges, wooden planks, and such things become entirely useless. It is the same for those who have seen their nature and awakened to the Way.
Thus, Dadian said: "It is like a blind person seeking a physician; unable to travel the long road by himself, he must rely on someone to lead him and, moreover, require a staff in his hand.
Only with these two things can he proceed; without them, he cannot reach his destination.
Once he arrives at the physician’s house, the physician applies ointment to his eyes, and he sees great radiance; at that point, both the staff and the person leading him are no longer needed."
The sudden awakening to the true path of Nirvana in its place of application is also like this.
Tell me, what is it that leads people? I shall now reveal it for you: those who believe shall simply act. External practice cannot easily accomplish internal realization;
one must extensively cultivate fields of merit. When merit arrives, the spirit becomes enlightened, and naturally there will be a path. This very thing is it.
Only after leading others can one sit in meditation, cultivate the Way, discern internal mastery, and seek the method for realizing the nature to resolve the great matter of birth and death.
Once the work is perfected in a single day and one beholds one's original face, that itself is the staff.
Yet, one must further visit enlightened masters, true worthies, and eminent monks to seek their certification and seal.

The Master said: "One who realizes the Truth is indeed a physician. One day he attained sudden enlightenment and realized that all the various expedient means of the past were entirely useless, with the sole exception that the staff must not be discarded.
The Daoist says: "When one has caught the fish, one forgets the wicker trap;

when one has caught the hare, one forgets the snare. The Buddhist says: "To cross the river, one must use a raft; once on the shore, the boat is no longer needed. The Confucian says: "When one has grasped the meaning, [the words are forgotten]."
"Forgotten the words, one obtains rice; forgotten the field, one obtains grain. But tell me, why does he instruct everyone to forget everything, yet alone not instruct them to discard the staff?
"Before reaching the place where the water ends and the mountains exhaust themselves, keep it as a companion to pass the time"—have you even begun to understand this?
This staff has no marks from the beginning; It is fundamentally no different from empty space.
If one can lift it up and penetrate the three heavens, The demons and spirits throughout the world will not dare to look upon it.
*Mahāmaitrī*.
*Mitra* is a Sanskrit term from the Western Heavens; in the Eastern Land, it is translated as *Wuji* (Ultimatelessness).
Now, as for *Wuji*, it is ultimateless, yet it is the *Taiji* (Supreme Ultimate). This is the wondrous Way of empty space. An ancient said: "From *Wuji* comes *Taiji*;

*Taiji* divides into the Two Polarities (*Eryi*); the Two Polarities divide into the Three Powers (*Sandai*); the Three Powers give birth to the Four Images (*Sixiang*); the Four Images give birth to..."
Because the Five Elements exist, the Five Elements gradually give rise to the myriad categories of beings;
all these categories are fully contained within the wondrous Way. Therefore, the single character "honey" is used as a metaphor for empty space and the wondrous Way.
The term "many" refers to the various classes of sentient and non-sentient beings, all of which belong to the encompassing embrace of the Way. It is just like a bee gathering [pollen].

When honey is being brewed from a hundred flowers and has not yet been completed, there are the various flavors of salty, sour, sweet, bitter, and pungent, and the various colors of blue, yellow, red, and white;
these flavors are unequal and these colors are not uniform.
Once the work of a single day is finished and the honey is accomplished, all the various flavors are fermented into a single flavor, and all the diverse colors blend together into a single fragrance.
Regarding fragrance and exquisite flavor, there is no difference whatsoever; when they reach this state, the bees obtain sustenance and people obtain enjoyment.

It is the same for those who practice the Way. For instance, when a practitioner disciplines body and mind, grinding them morning and evening, yet their meritorious practice has not yet reached completion, they may still harbor thoughts of stinginess and greed, a desire for profit and fame, or feelings of jealousy.
A calculating mind, a competitive mind, a conceited mind, a mind of self-importance, a murderous mind, a cruel mind,
a mind of the three poisons, a fearful mind, a deviant mind, a deluded mind, a mind of ignorance and darkness, and various other unwholesome minds;
furthermore, a violent and evil nature, a coarse and impetuous nature, a fickle nature like the wind, a nature that follows what is heterodox, a dull and turbid nature— [such] views.
The nature of the realms, the nature of inferiority, the nature of falsehood, the nature of fondness for strife, the nature of stubbornness,

the nature of madness, the nature of frivolity, and the nature of flattery— these and all other habitual tendencies from beginningless kalpas, numbering more than eighty-four thousand, cannot be fully described.
When the work of a single day is perfected, the stubborn mind is naturally exhausted, and one is forged into the singular flavor of supreme purity.
Above, the unimpeded true mind, through various self-refinement, accomplishes a single, perfect, and luminous *dharmatā* that remains indestructible for ten thousand kalpas.
Upon reaching this state, there is neither a mind of differentiation nor a nature of diverse categories;
all evils naturally dissolve and all evils naturally perish, as the single truth alone is revealed, attaining great sovereignty. As an ancient worthy said: "The myriad stars..."
The bright clarity of the sun is not equal to the solitary brilliance of the lone moon. The Way says: "The hundred rivers flow on without end, yet the single sea receives them all without limit.
The Immortal Master said: "A thousand thoughts and ten thousand anxieties ultimately result in delusion; guard alone in stillness that which is True, and the Way will naturally draw near.
But tell me, how does one come to see that One Truth? *Pah!* With eyes wide open, you are deceived by it.
The multitude cannot grasp it; have you even glimpsed it?
Its various and manifold aspects are difficult to fathom—do not let them wander hither and thither in differentiation.
Gather them in and place them within the cinnabar furnace, refining them until they glow as red as the golden sun.
"Time. Time is the time of right view. To speak of 'seeing' is to say there is nothing to be seen; to speak of 'time' is to say the time cannot yet be fixed.
As the Immortal Master said: "At the very moment the first yang moves, there is naturally an inexhaustible message."—The Ancient Virtuous One.
The clouds part and the clear wind rustles, penetrating the heart; at such a time, this joy is difficult for others to know.

It is the mystery within mysteries, without east, west, south, or north, nor the four intermediate directions, above or below, nor past, future, or present. Within the equality of empty space, it blends indistinguishably with the Great Way, returning together to a single moment. —From the *Chuán* (Stream) [of the *Zuòwáng zhì*] Note: The term "玄之又玄" (*xuán zhī yòu xuán*) is a famous phrase from the *Dào dé jīng* (Classic of the Way and Its Power), signifying the profoundest level of the mysterious and ineffable.

The passage describes a state of non-dual realization where all temporal and spatial distinctions dissolve into the undifferentiated unity of the Great Way. The final line, "共歸一時" (*gòng guī yī shí*), indicates that all things return together to the same single moment of ultimate reality. The title "川" (*chuān*, Stream) likely refers to a specific section or chapter of the source text.

The Old Man says: "At all times, the clear breeze and bright moon accompany him; when asked about the peach blossoms' red, the plum blossoms' white, and the roses' purple, the Lord of the East knows nothing at all.
Tell me, where does the Lord of the East take his stand? Do you see him? He cannot be struck away, nor can he be cut to death.
He is within the red of the peach and the white of the plum; he is within the yellow of the rose.
Purple—He-he! Have you grasped it yet?
If one asks precisely when it was, the clear breeze and bright moon are known by oneself.
Last night the Master of the East transmitted a message; the first branch of the red plum has burst into bloom.

Regarding "having a form that accords with the Way," "form" (*rūpa*) carries the meaning of obstruction. If, upon encountering objects or meeting external conditions, one is neither attached nor defiled, this is the absence of obstruction;
thus, the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) is naturally empty. Regarding "feeling" (*vedanā*), it carries the meaning of reception.

If, when meeting all realms of sound and form, the mind does not receive or grasp them, the aggregate of feeling (*vedanāskandha*) is empty. Regarding "perception" (*saṃjñā*), it refers to conceptual construction.

The meaning of "contemplation" (*si-lü*) is that one does not contemplate the past, has no thoughts regarding the future, and remains naturally as it is in the present, thereby realizing the emptiness of the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*).

The meaning of the practitioner’s mental attention (*citta-manasikāra*) being unceasing is that throughout the twelve periods of the day, the mind does not wander outward, the thoughts are not distracted or chaotic, and one is neither turned by external objects nor detained by sensory conditions; thus, not a single thought departs from this state.
In the very place where they arise, one realizes that perceptions are empty. One who understands this knows there is no sense of intimacy or estrangement;

it is simply the principle of responding to phenomena. If one sees all objects and circumstances without any discrimination or recognition, viewing them all with uniform equanimity—seeing as if not seeing, knowing as if not knowing—then there is neither intimacy nor estrangement.
When things come, respond to them; when they go, do not dwell on them.
One attains the emptiness of the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*). Having reached this state, one naturally perceives that all five aggregates are empty;
the six windows [of the senses] are bright and pure, utterly naked and vividly clear, with nothing to grasp.
Furthermore, even the names "four great elements" and "five aggregates" cannot be found. The Master said, "One sees only emptiness. The Commentary says, "Empty space."
Unveiled and Alone: Once, while King Kali was out hunting, he encountered an immortal sage. When the king questioned him, the sage did not answer;

first he withdrew his left shoulder, then he exposed his right arm, and as the king dismembered him limb by limb, the sage’s face showed no sign of fear or anger, remaining exactly as it had always been without changing expression.
Later, the King of Kaśmīra asked the Venerable Siṃha:
"What are you doing here? the Venerable replied, "I am here [to realize] the emptiness of the aggregates. The Dharma King asked, "Have you attained the emptiness of the aggregates?
The Venerable replied, "I have already attained the emptiness of the aggregates. The Dharma King said, "Can you get your teacher's head? The Venerable replied, "The body is not mine;
how much less so the head? Furthermore, Master Zhao said: "The four great elements are originally non-existent."
"My five aggregates are entirely empty; to bring my head before a white blade is like cutting the spring breeze.
Furthermore, when Śāriputra saw the goddess and asked why she did not change out of her female body, the goddess replied:
"For twelve years I have sought a female body and could not find it at all. What, then, would you have me change? From the patriarchs of old...

The Master had attained the dharma of the emptiness of the aggregates. Furthermore, when the Venerable Jingqing was in charge of the monastery for three years, the local deity of the temple could not find an opportunity to see the Master’s countenance.

Moreover, while the immortal Huo Taigu was practicing the Way beneath the bridge at Zhaozhou, he suddenly heard a group of ghosts conversing by the riverbank one night, saying: "Tomorrow there will be one..."
The man wearing the iron cap finished speaking on my behalf, and thereafter there was no further sound or sign. When evening fell on the following day, a heavy rain suddenly began;
I saw a man carrying an iron cauldron upon his head to shield himself from the rain, who had come to the foot of the bridge intending to wash his feet.
As he was about to cross, Taigu saw him and shouted, "You must not wash! Hearing the True Man’s words, the man supported himself against the railing.
He crossed the bridge and departed; by nightfall, all the ghosts had arrived.
One ghost said, "I have waited three years for a substitute head, yet this gentleman has taken mine away and destroyed it.
The ghosts wished to harm the True Man, but as they searched for him while he was traveling back and forth, they could not find him. Not knowing where the True Man was, they sighed and departed.

At that time, the True Man remained beneath the bridge, yet the ghost could not see him. Furthermore, when National Teacher Hongjue was staying in his hermitage, the celestial kitchen sent food to him;
later, after he had visited Master Dongshan and returned to the hermitage, the deity sent food for three days.

When the deity arrived at the hermitage and did not see the master, why was it that the master—who was actually right there in the hermitage—could not be seen? All such cases are obtainable [as examples].
The Dharma of Sudden and Perfect Enlightenment and the secret method for concealing the body are such that neither spirits nor ghosts can perceive them. Now tell me:
the four elements are not substantial, the physical body does not exist, and the five aggregates are entirely empty—this is truly one's original face.
*Tut!* From where does this single phrase emerge? Who is it that clearly perceives the emptiness of the five aggregates?
The blind fellow misses it right before his eyes! *Ei!* With one’s whole mind fixed only upon the fishing line, one fails to see the reeds facing the red smartweed. Do you see?
Once you have recognized this and turned back, you shall immediately apply yourself to practice; then, with clear realization and liberation, you will awaken to the emptiness of the mind.
When the four great elements of another have all fallen away, there remains within them a distinct spiritual power that delivers one from all suffering and calamity.
If one realizes the emptiness of the five aggregates, one then transcends the realm of birth and death and escapes the suffering of saṃsāra. Thus says the Most High:
"I have a great affliction because I have a body; were I without a body, what affliction would I have?
The Buddhist commentary says: "The body is the root of all suffering. The Confucian says: "With a body there is affliction; without attachment there is no sorrow. The Sūtra says:
"The three realms offer no peace, like a burning house filled with manifold sufferings—how truly terrifying they are! If it is thus...
A person of wisdom reflects back upon themselves and realizes that their own body is entirely illusory and not real;
how much more so other things? When the impermanence of a single day arrives, everything will be cast aside, and not one thing will be of any use.

If one maintains this mindfulness at every thought, the dualistic mind will naturally vanish and distracting thoughts will naturally diminish. Furthermore, one must visit and seek out spiritual teachers, drawing near to those who possess true wisdom.
Seeking the path of liberation and resolving the great matter of life and death, one day with a sudden "pop," the bottom of the lacquer bucket falls away, and one beholds one's original face.
Do you wish to see your original face? It has never changed throughout the ages;
it is only that people themselves fail to recognize it as true.
If one attains the emptiness of mind, suffering ceases to exist; what birth and death could there be, and what constraints?
Having once cast off the swaddling clothes of the womb, one becomes a carefree Great Man. Śāriputra!

"House" refers to the physical dwelling. The "beneficial son," who is the true spirit originally present within the house of the four elements and five aggregates that presides over this physical frame, is like the host of an inn who stays for a time.
If the host leaves the house, the structure collapses; yet the beneficial son remains constant, merely changing his residence.
Regarding "Dwelling," Dao said: "The body is the abode of qi, and the mind is the residence of the spirit;
after a long time, the spirit and qi disperse, which is like moving house and dwelling elsewhere. Shi explained: "Since beginningless kalpas, we have lived as tenants in this house until now;
who recognizes the true host? Yaoshan further said: "When skin and flesh have fallen away entirely, there remains only the single reality."
Do you wish to see the true reality? Do you yet recognize this circle (○)?
Coming and going thousands of times, it is merely that worldly people have failed to grasp its form.
Do not say that the chamber is not spacious enough; it encompasses heaven, earth, and the mountains and rivers.
Within it dwells a true immortal, untainted by even a speck of dust, eternally abiding in the Great Brahma Heaven.
His form is no different from emptiness.
The nature of the Way is non-dual; form and emptiness are one and the same, ever present before one’s eyes, manifesting forms in response to things.
Yet all people fail to recognize it: when space is long, it is long space; when short, it is short space. When square, it is square space;
when round, it is round space. When white, it is white space; when red, it is red space. When small, it is small space; when large, it is large space. When distant, it is distant space.
The Chan [Zen] master says: "That which is near is near to emptiness. The Daoist says: "Every person inherently possesses it; each and every one lacks nothing. The Buddhist says:
"All sentient beings, down to the crawling insects, possess Buddha-nature. The Confucian says: "All sentient beings are each endowed with a single Great Ultimate (Tàijí).
An ancient worthy further said: "In every atom there is the Way; in every atom there is the Buddha. The Immortal and the Perfected One say: "What thing is it?"
If one does not receive the Way, where is there that is not the transformation of the Way? It manifests its form wherever it is, acting with sovereign ease;
the Way is not far from people—it is people themselves who distance themselves from it. Look back at your own body: within this form, there must be the true emptiness of awakened nature.
That which responds and appears in various forms is precisely what is manifested by the true emptiness of awakened nature. Yongjia said:
The illusory, empty body is itself the Dharma-body; the Dharma-body, through awakening, realizes there is not a single thing—it is the original source-nature, the true and heavenly Buddha.
The Immortal Zhen said: "Within the provisional form of having shape, the true form of no-shape is contained.
Master Bao said: "Within the body that has marks, there is the body without marks. *Du!* Do you understand? Peach blossoms red, willows green.
Green willows and red blossoms, plum flowers and white; all are the transformative work of the Lord of Spring.
The creation of empty space is naturally skillful; the great earth, mountains, and rivers are a harmoniously fused essence.
Manifesting forms everywhere, people do not recognize them; they themselves remain ignorant of their own true host.
Emptiness is not different from form;
form and emptiness are not of one kind, yet worldly people differentiate them for themselves. The Daoist says: "The Great Square has no corners;
it is a homogenous single body. The Buddhist says: "The entire trichiliocosm is unified into a single world. The Confucian says: "Ascending the Eastern Mountain."
Standing atop Mount Tai, one makes the world seem small; casting aside the thick weeds, what is this and what is that? The ancients said:
"The sages and saints always practice the wisdom of equality and do not give rise to marks of discrimination. The sages and saints of the Three Teachings are also empty;
the four modes of birth and the six realms of existence are also empty; from the highest immortals and Buddhas down to the most minute insects and grasses.

Each and every tree is fundamentally and originally empty. Before the Great Simplicity had dispersed, before Yin and Yang were divided, before the Two Polarities were distinguished, and before the Three Powers were established—what "self" could there have been? Originally, it was all one single principle.

Because the Great Simplicity dispersed, heaven and earth conjoined, the Three Powers were established, and the myriad things came into being and flourished, continuing until this very day without ceasing.
Why must one return to the source? It is simply because sentient beings cling to appearances and do not know that, from the beginning, all is empty.
They delude themselves by pursuing external objects, giving rise to inverted views as they drift with the flow of phenomena and fail to return to the One. Their faculties and perspectives differ;

some cling to form, others to emptiness, following these two views of form and emptiness. If a person can, within this state,豁然 (huòrán—suddenly and expansively) realize emptiness, their body and mind will become equal.
Within and without, there is nothing remaining; one does not perceive emptiness or form, is not driven by things, and is not deceived by circumstances.
All is uniformly equal—wherein could there be even "one"? Thus, one immediately returns to the source. Yet, even this "one" is excessive. The Patriarch Chongyang said:
"Embracing the Origin and Guarding the One is the practice. Through the long duration of earth and heaven, even "one" is non-existent. — Ancient Sage.
It is said that the myriad dharmas return to the One; to what does the One return? You must know the place where the One returns.
Now tell me, where does the One return? *Ei!* A dog licking a hot oil pan—do you understand?
Neither man nor ox is seen; their traces are utterly lost. All say that coming from emptiness is not empty.
A single mass of white clouds returns to its source, Leaving only the bright moon to illuminate the vast sky.
Form is itself emptiness.
Emptiness exists within form, yet it is difficult for people of the world to perceive. The eye is form and cannot see objects; it is only the wondrous capacity of true emptiness that can see.
The ear is form and cannot hear sounds; it is only the wondrous capacity of true emptiness that can hear.
The nose is form and cannot discern fragrances or stenches; it is only the wondrous capacity of true emptiness that can discern them. The tongue is form...
The inability to speak is simply the wondrous nature of true emptiness; the body is form, yet it is simply the wondrous nature of true emptiness that is able to speak.
The inability to perceive touch is simply the wondrous nature of true emptiness; the feet are form, yet it is simply the wondrous nature of true emptiness that is able to walk.
The hands are form, yet it is simply the wondrous nature of true emptiness that is able to grasp and take up things.

One can pick up and set down; yet within the wondrous nature of true emptiness, there are no eyes that can see, no ears that can hear, no nose that can smell, no tongue that can speak, no feet that can walk, and no hands that can grasp.
The faculty of mind has a name but no form;
its eighty-four thousand modes of seeing, hearing, knowing, and perceiving all ultimately return to the six sense organs, functioning interchangeably throughout the entire body.
The wondrous function of supernormal powers—ancients said it is "the whole body is it" and "everywhere is it"; the Way says there is no need to search far elsewhere.
Throughout the twelve hours of the day, it pervades the entire body. Form and emptiness are not different; the subtle principle is fully manifest.
What can be called form is not true form; what can be called emptiness is not true emptiness. All returns to the Great Emptiness. And so it is.
"What do you say to this principle? Master Chuan said: "To have form and to seek are both delusions;

to be formless and shadowless is to fall into partiality and desiccation. How could there ever be an interval between the majestic and the subtle? A single path of cold light pierces the great void. The *Laozi* says:
"To know emptiness as not empty, and to know form as not form—this is called illumination and realization. I now do not...
I spare you the tedious explanation: if you encounter any object with form, do not allow yourself to become stained by attachment;

if you reach the state where emotions are forgotten and thoughts are severed, do not allow yourself to be deluded regarding the Truth or attached to forms. To be attached to existence is to cling to being; to be deluded regarding the Truth is to fall into emptiness.
Only when you neither cling to emptiness nor cling to existence are you a person who has truly understood. Do you understand? Cease!
When you feel drowsy, wake yourself up!
All ten thousand apertures are opened by way of a single aperture; that one aperture can contain the vast void of space.
If you can grasp this mysterious aperture within the midst of mystery, with a wave of the hand, all shall return to the Great Way.
Emptiness is form; form exists within emptiness.
Otherwise, people are deceived by external objects. The Immortal Zhen said: "Without the Way, the myriad phenomena cannot manifest;
without the Way, the myriad phenomena cannot arise. The Commentary says: "To see form is to see emptiness; there is no form apart from emptiness."
In emptiness, nothing is seen; therefore, the sages and worthies of the Three Teachings do not see form as existing or emptiness as existing.
Form and emptiness are both extinguished, and there is no distinction between internal and external; suchness is eternally spontaneous, its luminous brilliance penetrating and pervading all lands.
Worldly people, however, are not thus; they argue about the internal and the external, and speak of "that" and "this," clinging to appearances and making discriminatory views.
Chasing after various forms and following along with sounds, one is deluded regarding the Truth and remains unaware.

Emerging from the shell and entering the shell, one wanders on without knowing how to change one's head or alter one's face; there will be no end to this. It is not a matter concerning others, but something you have sought out for yourself.
Why do you not turn back early to save yourself? Tell me, how can one be saved? *Du!* (A shout) Let it go! Follow along!
The former evil water-jar is like a golden needle applied to the site of pain;
it is uniformly even, with no disparity whatsoever.
Originally, it was all one's own home, yet because one clings to the tips of the branches, one has lost sight of the sprout of the Great Way from long ago.

Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness arise because of seeing with the eye; because of feeling form, there is perception; because of perception, there are mental formations; because of mental formations, there is consciousness.
With the six sense organs as cause, the six objects are produced; thus, from a single consciousness, there are four [aggregates].

Within these great five aggregates, there exists this physical body of the five aggregates; thus, one becomes attached to and distinguishes between appearances, following after sounds and pursuing forms, from which hatred, love, sorrow, and fear arise.
Consequently, one wanders through birth and death without ceasing.

If you wish to sever birth and death and bring an end to the cycle of saṃsāra, you must simply use the light of a single faculty to penetrate the source from which they arise, thereby shattering the four elements and the five [aggregates].
The aggregates are utterly exhausted and vast emptiness is devoid of self; right now, one is empty and still.

Accepting this directly, one realizes that prior to the kalpa of emptiness, one’s own nature is a circle (○) that is "still yet constantly illuminating, illuminating yet constantly still. The Supreme One said: "If there is stillness, there is nothing to be stilled.
How could desire lead to longevity? When desire does not arise, this is true stillness. He further said: "One sees only emptiness."
Contemplating emptiness, one finds that emptiness itself is empty and there is nothing to be emptied. Since that which is emptied is non-existent, even "non-existence" is non-existent.

When non-existence is also non-existent, all is profoundly still and eternally quiescent. The commentary states: "The person is empty and phenomena are empty; these two aspects are fundamentally identical.
Furthermore, since both person and phenomena are empty, where exactly does one abide? All objective realms and myriad conditions leave no trace.
Abiding, one is indistinctly hidden within the great void.
The eye-faculty drags along the myriad realms in their bustle; when one sees nothing desirable, all conditions are forgotten.
When there is nothing to forget, the whole body emerges, and one immediately beholds the Great Dharma King of the Spirit Mountain.
It is likewise so.
Once there is no self, then all phenomena are non-existent; returning once more to emptiness, one attains the restoration of the source and the return to the origin.
In the Buddha-dharma this is called "all phenomena return to the One"; in the Way of the Daoists it is called "returning life to the root."
The Confucians call this the restoration of the primordial *tianli* (Heavenly Principle).
Here, words are cut off and the mind’s activities cease. If you stir a thought, you deviate; if you make an arrangement, it is not so.
Therefore, Old Shuanshan said: "Step back! Step back! Look—this stubborn rock moves! Do you understand? *Du!* Desist!
If you get up and run away, you will receive thirty blows of the staff.
The moment a single thought arises, appearances are already formed; To describe reality is to pursue delusion and obscure the path home.
If you can let go so that all is empty and void, You will proceed steadily within the Tathāgatagarbha.
Śāriputra, one cannot recognize fire face-to-face, for it cannot burn; one cannot drown in water, for it cannot submerge;
an arrow cannot wound, a sword cannot cleave, the wind cannot blow away, the sun cannot scorch, and the rain cannot drench; it cannot be depicted in painting, nor can it be neutralized by poison.
Evil insects cannot harm you nor sting you; it is only because your path of travel has gone astray that you have lost the *pāramitās*.
Do you see Śāriputra? From antiquity until now, he has never changed;
he merely comes and goes, renting houses to dwell in—sometimes in vermilion towers and painted pavilions, sometimes in thatched huts and straw halls, and sometimes...
Golden screens and vermilion doors are sometimes broken; the shrine niches of the temple kiln—do you perceive them? The Old Man of Chuan said:
"Clouds rise on the South Mountain, rain falls on the North Mountain; horse, donkey, mule—how many kinds are there? Look at the vast and impassive waters:
in some places they follow the contours, in others they are round. If you wish to avoid coming and going, you must attain freedom from all outflows (*āsrava*).

Having exhausted [all conditioned things], one returns to quiescent extinction; such a person has not yet departed from the triple world, yet neither heaven nor earth can constrain them, becoming a carefree man beyond all things.
Do you understand? It is better to retreat than to press forward; it is better to be natural than to force and manipulate.
The master within one's own room dwells together with you, yet you do not know his whereabouts.
If you can step back and look within, you will encounter him in every object and at every turn;
this is the empty nature of all phenomena.
All dharmas are empty; originally they are not the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*). The Immortal Sage said: "Dharmas are fundamentally no-dharmas;
forms are fundamentally no-forms. That which has form is ultimately false; that which is signless is the true person. The *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* says:
"Even dharmas should be relinquished, how much more so non-dharmas. It also says: "All that has marks is entirely illusory. If one perceives all..."

To see that marks are non-marks is to see the Tathāgata. Those former masters who spoke of "emptiness" with one flavor did so solely because sentient beings are, from the very outset, burdened by emptiness and fail to practice it;
thus, they established various provisional names to guide them, so that both the animate and the inanimate might all return to empty stillness and regain their original source.
If your faith has not yet reached this point, simply retire to sit in quietude and reflect.
Shiningly one perceives that the five aggregates are truly non-existent; naturally, one forgets form and forgets substance, thereby attaining the emptiness of persons.

Once the emptiness of persons is attained, just as when a disease is cured the medicine is naturally discarded, so too are phenomena empty. When both person and phenomenon are empty, one naturally comes to rest and ceases all striving.
As the Sūtra says: "My body is fundamentally non-existent; from what source could love or hatred arise? Since...
When one attains the state of forgetting form and forgetting the body, there are no further thoughts or concerns that can lead one to this ground; naturally, one lets go.
There is no Buddha or immortal to be made, no birth-and-death to be severed, no cultivation, and no realization.

If there were even a hair’s breadth more of cultivation or realization, one would fall into the realm of birth-and-death and suffer eternal sinking and wandering. Only if one can completely and thoroughly escape [from these] is it so.

Sprinkling [the mind] so that it has no place of dependence, not falling into the two extremes of existence and non-existence, standing alone like empty space, and directly taking responsibility for what was before the void kalpa—what is there that is not perfectly round, radiant, and brilliant? Do you understand?
Heaven and earth are two lotuses in the sea; all sentient beings emerge and submerge therein in vain.
When both person and phenomena are empty, the mind rests of its own accord; there is neither joy nor sorrow.
When the wind ceases and the waves subside, the clouds depart; the moon shines upon the cold river, all in one hue of autumn—neither arising nor ceasing.
That there is formation and destruction is the characteristic of phenomena; that there is neither birth nor cessation is the principle of nature.

This direct statement and direct teaching reveals that sentient beings are fully endowed with the Dharmakāya, the wondrous nature of true emptiness, which spans all time, never having been born and never having ceased, unchanging and immovable, without coming or going, without old and without new—sublime and majestic in this way! Great and Supreme One!
It is said: "Silent and vast, standing alone without changing, moving everywhere without weariness. It is also said: "Silent and unmoving, yet responding and penetrating all at once;
as for the four elements and five aggregates, let them arise and perish in vain according to others—it has no connection whatsoever with one's own *dharmakāya*.
But tell me, since there is no connection, how can it be that every step is not [in accord]?
Master Li said: "Harmonizing with the light of the mundane world, unstained by the three realms, he alone stands as the Honored One.
Master Chuan also said: "Where there is leisure, one should simply enjoy the leisure; clouds fly high and waters flow on their own.
We see only the black winds tossing great waves, yet we have never heard of the fishing boat being sunk. If this is so, tell me: is there a point of connection here?
There is no meeting or interaction. If one realizes that the five aggregates are all empty, what separation or non-separation could there be?
Do you understand this principle? The flowing water never stays still; the green mountains are ever at leisure.
Let the four elements come and go as they will; clouds arrive and clouds depart, yet they remain ever-present.
The shadows of bamboo sweep the steps, yet no dust is stirred; the moon pierces the bottom of the pond, yet the water leaves no trace.
Neither defiled nor pure.
It is also said that sentient beings are originally pure; their *dharmakāya* is nameless, signless, traceless, flawless, and unstained.
It is neither living nor non-living, neither long nor short, neither square nor round. It cannot be destroyed and cannot be burned, like empty space.
It is like a lotus flower that is not adhered to by water—neither defiled nor pure—remaining thus eternally throughout all kalpas.
Like the moon in the water—do you wish to see it? It radiates light wherever it goes; how many people can truly behold it?
The one Dharma-body is pure and without blemish, like a lotus emerging from the water, unsullied by dust.
Its manifestations appear throughout the waters of a thousand rivers, yet these thousand moons are none other than the reality of the single moon.
Neither increasing nor decreasing—how could the substance of chaotic empty space, the body of the distant kalpa of emptiness, be increased? How could it be decreased?
It cannot be harmed, nor can it be benefited. The Way says: "It is present in the sages without being in excess."
"Ordinary and without deficiency. The commentary states: "Suchness is spontaneous, neither deficient nor redundant. It further states: "It endures through kalpas without perishing;
it reaches back to antiquity without shifting. An ancient master said: "Its essence is like empty space, boundless and shoreless.
Bodhisattvas of the Supreme Vehicle will believe in it without doubt, but those of the middle and lower capacities will surely find it strange. Furthermore:
"Why is the Way thus? Hehe! Your own rope is too short, yet you blame the well for being deep;
this is truly your own fault. Tsk! You were already acquainted on Vulture Peak—why do you fail to recognize me today?"
Regarding the Dharma-body and the form-body, there is no need to discuss whether they are distant or near;
all rely upon the power of the Eastern Lord. Flowers and willows alike experience the spring;
thus it is within emptiness.
The wondrous Dharma is true emptiness: neither arising nor ceasing, neither defiled nor pure; it cannot increase and cannot decrease.
It is primordially pure, unchanged through past and present, and eternally abiding for ten thousand kalpas. Swords cannot cut it; arrows cannot pierce it; ropes cannot bind it; fire cannot burn it;
rain cannot moisten it; pushing or pulling does not displace it; striking it— (Note: The provided text ends abruptly; this is a translation of the portion available.)
It is difficult to grasp it because it is painful to seize; why is this so? It is because these things do not obstruct empty space, and empty space does not obstruct things.
The Immortal Zhen said: "True emptiness does not hang upon things; the Great Way is not stained by dust. Master Chuan said:
"Empty space does not obstruct even a hair’s breadth of thought; therefore, he is manifested as the Great Awakened Immortal. This is the True Text of Wenshi.
The Sūtra says: "Though heaven and earth are vast, they cannot sprout a seed-kernel suspended in space;
though yin and yang are subtle, they cannot produce an egg from a female without a male. Now tell me, for what reason can heaven and earth not bring forth creation?
Why is it that yin and yang cannot transform things suspended in space, and why can they not sprout [a kernel] that does not touch the soil? It is because it lacks the foundation of the earth.
Attached to objective realms, one lacks the seed of the Hero; that which cannot bring about transformation is empty within and devoid of substance.
Do you understand? Inwardly and outwardly, it is utterly empty; ghosts and spirits cannot seize it.
In true emptiness, not even a speck of dust is established; As soon as there is a speck of dust, it is no longer real.
Having cast off both the mud and the water and stripped away the cloth robe, One clearly sees the person within:
Without form, feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.

Since these five aggregates exist within emptiness as accumulated habits, they rest within the substance of empty space: resting in form, it does not receive form; resting in sound, it does not receive sound;
resting in sensation, it does not receive sensation; resting in perception, it does not receive perception; resting in mental formations, it does not receive mental formations;
resting in consciousness, it does not receive consciousness. All provisional names and provisional marks of the six paths and four modes of birth are entirely without reception.
Receiving the pure, empty, and wondrous Way, not even a speck of dust can be established; ultimately it is formless. Walking is like the path of a bird;
sitting is like the great void. But tell me, what is meant by the "bird-path" and the "great void"?
Heh! Though one walks the bird-path, no trace is seen; though the true void is revealed, no mark is seen. Do you understand?
When the five aggregates are all absent, one perceives emptiness; why seek the master elsewhere?
Once the water is clear, the fish appear of themselves; in every instance, there is no obscuration, for spiritual power is present.
There are no eyes, ears, nose, tongue, body, or mind.
Now tell me: what is this state where there are no eyes, ears, nose, tongue, body, or mind? Do not remain idle and watch, lest you miss it. I shall now explain clearly:
when these six sense organs exist, they constitute the physical body; when these six consciousnesses are absent, it is called the Dharma-body.
Such a person is merely one who practices cultivation; though their eyes see, they do not become attached to it.
Though the ears hear forms, do not become attached to sounds; though the nose smells, do not become attached to fragrances or odors;
though the tongue tastes, do not become attached to flavors; though one possesses a body, one must refrain from becoming attached to its appearance;
one must forget both form and substance; and though the mind responds to affairs, it must not become attached to external objects.
The Supreme Way requires that one should always remain tranquil. The Daoists say: "The eyes do not gaze upon forms; the ears do not listen to sounds; the tongue does not crave flavors;
the nose does not smell fragrances; the body does not move recklessly; and the mind does not become deranged. The Confucians say: "Do not look at what is contrary to propriety;
do not listen to what is contrary to propriety; do not speak what is contrary to propriety; and do not move in a manner contrary to propriety. This is precisely having no eyes or ears.

The nose, tongue, body, and mind are likewise the purification of the six sense organs (*ṣaḍ-indriya*), which is the non-defilement of the six sense objects (*ṣaḍ-viṣaya*), and furthermore, the emptiness of the six consciousnesses (*ṣaḍ-vijñāna*).
In summary, this is the stillness of the eighteen realms (*aṣṭādaśa-dhātu*).

It is also called the extinction of the six depletions and the death of the six thieves, wherein the one true reality remains unmoving. It is the closing of the gates of the six doors; in summary, it is the emptiness of the eighteen prisons.
When severance is like this, then paradise is near; one immediately perceives the original *dharmakāya*. Do you wish to see the original *dharmakāya*?
It is that which sees when in the eye, hears when in the ear, smells when in the nose, speaks when on the tongue, grasps when in the hand, and moves when in the foot.
It is the total manifestation of function; it is the total *dharmakāya*. Is it not so?

Regarding these six sense organs, four elements, and five aggregates, in seeing, hearing, knowing, and perceiving, one must strictly refrain from identifying the four elements and six sense organs as oneself.
The *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: "All that has marks is entirely empty and false. The Way says:
"The awakened forget thoughts and return to the truth; the deluded cling to marks and lose their original nature. All of these are provisional names used to guide sentient beings.
Birth is unknowable; to attain realization, one must personally see the Dharmakāya. If one attains personal vision, one transforms from an ordinary being into a sage.

To rely on the spoken words of others or intellectual understanding derived from texts is like trying to satisfy hunger with a painted cake or quench thirst by talking about wine—it will never suffice for the task at hand.
Regarding the phrase "Flowers in the medicinal railing," do not be negligent or superficial.
"The scale lies in the beam, not in the pan. The Patriarch Chongyang said, "Do not allow yourself to mistake the fixed mark on the scale.
Now tell me, how is this statement to be explained? It means that while the pan can only balance objects, it is the marks upon the beam that distinguish light from heavy.
The Patriarch further feared that people would mistake the fixed mark on the scale and seek a definitive standard therein.
The scale-pan is a dead thing that knows nothing of lightness or heaviness; therefore, do not mistakenly fixate on the scale-pan.
Generally speaking, there are scales that are useful and those that are not; these all serve as metaphors for the Dharma.
Examine them with subtle precision; do not cling to one side. But tell me, what is this principle? It is the True Nature and...
The true spirit of the nature of consciousness dwells together with the conscious spirit; one is false and one is real.
Fix your gaze firmly: when a heron flies up from within the snow, you will finally know.
There is but one lock for six gates; there is no need to further bar the five doors.
Let the affairs of the world remain in their chaotic turmoil; the Honored Patriarch within the hall remains ever at peace.
There is no form, sound, fragrance, taste, touch, or mental object.
These are the six sense objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*), all of which arise from a single faculty. Simply turn back and reflect upon that single faculty: from where do they arise?
If you identify the place of their arising, they originate from the root; since that place of arising is delusion, cease its growth. As the Immortal Shen Zhen said:
"Stirring the broth to cool the bubbles is not as good as drawing out the firewood from the bottom of the cauldron. The commentary says: one must cut it down.
As for that tree, first remove its roots and branches; they will naturally fall away. Once you have identified the fundamental source, discard the provisional and return to the real.
Recognize that this body of yours is not a self-existent body; since even the myriad phenomena are empty, they are naturally pure and still.

Contemplate the body as being without a body, and contemplate phenomena in the same way. All things return to emptiness and quiescence. Furthermore, sit in stillness and contemplate what was done in the past.
Where do these manifold forms, sounds, fragrances, tastes, tangibles, and mental objects reside? Since they are ultimately non-existent, they are like last night’s dream.
My own mind is fundamentally empty; neither merit nor sin has a master. What, then, is sin? What is merit?
The Sūtra says: "To contemplate with clarity that the offenses of the mind are originally empty—this is what is called true repentance.
Now tell me, what does one repent of, and what does one regret? To repent is to repent for one's past errors; to regret is to not commit them again.
*Du!* (A shout) Since all the sense-faculties have been severed, where can sprouts grow? There is only emptiness.
"Space exists. Do you wish to see this void? You cannot see it; you cannot grasp its form.
It stands face-to-face before you, constantly radiant and brilliant. Have you recognized it yet?
All phenomena are empty; there is neither sin nor merit.
One must further sit in stillness until, in a sudden flash, one seizes the hand of Vairocana. To be a true man, a great hero:
no realm of the eye, and so on, up to no realm of consciousness.
If the eye-element (*cakṣurdhātu*) is purified, consciousness will find rest and these eighteen elements will naturally become peaceful.

These eighteen elements are unsettled because of the grasping that there is an eye-element; they are entangled by this attachment. Simply by removing the eye-faculty (*cakṣurindriya*), one returns to investigate its falsity.
As the ancient masters said: "The eye is an obstacle to the Way; when the demonic army clings to objects, one becomes deluded and loses the way back."—The Immortal and the Perfected One.

It is said: "When the eye observes and the mind moves, one becomes attached to objects and loses sight of the Truth. This body is not an entry [into reality]; all six sense organs return to decay and ruin.
If one quietly examines the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), they possess no substantial meaning whatsoever.

There exists only the wondrous nature of true emptiness, a body that does not perish throughout long eons, serene and eternally present, requiring neither cultivation nor realization. The Śākya [Buddha] said: "The Nāga remains forever in meditative concentration; there is no arising or ceasing."
There is a time of indeterminacy. The former masters said: "The realm within meditative concentration is the *qiankun* (Heaven and Earth) within stillness;
it occurs spontaneously and is not something produced through effort. Once one has attained the power of concentration, how could there be any distraction?
