It is like the autumn moon—perfectly round, its light shining brightly, illuminating everywhere across heaven and earth, with no place that is not reached. Thus it is said.
This illumination is also spontaneous, for it is not produced by deliberate conceptualization. Shide further said:
"My mind is not like the moon; the moon has its waxing and waning, but a lamp without oil illuminates the ten directions through and through.
Mountains, rivers, and the great earth cannot obstruct it; its radiance is brilliantly clear, utterly transcending the sense organs and their objects, revealing the true permanence of the essence."
Utterly free from defilement, simply being detached from all conditions is itself the state of the Immortals and Buddhas. Do you understand?
The luminosity is complete without the slightest lack; one only fears the clouds that arise to obscure it.
When encountering circumstances, if there is no mental eye, then clarity arises. By turning back to observe oneself, one sees the path ahead.
The numinous light shoots through the roads of Chang’an; Alone one proceeds upon the path to Penglai.
There is no ignorance.

"No ignorance" means that the myriad conditions do not arise. Ignorance is the dark, incessant state of mind. One— *Note: The final character "一" (one) appears to be a fragment of a subsequent line or a concluding marker.*
All sentient beings without exception possess the cause of ignorance (*avidyā*). Because of ignorance, manifold and diverse afflictions (*kleśa*) arise;
these are all states of a darkened mind, and for this reason [the path] is thus described. The *Commentary* says: "The darkened mind does not cease;
its root is hell and the animal realm. The *Explanation* says: "Because of ignorance, one does not see the path to Bodhi; unaware, one leads one's own body [astray]."
Falling into the Pit of Fire: The Confucians say that when the inch-sized mind is not obscured, all dharmas are clear.
Furthermore, Guangchengzi said: "When wood is separated from fire, it does not turn to ash; when a person is free from passion, they do not die. Dadian said:

"The mind dwelling amidst the six passions is like a bird cast into a net; creating evil karma is like a moth rushing into a lamp; emerging from the shell only to enter it again, revolving in transmigration."

Thus, one revolves through the cycle of wandering for kalpas without awakening; all this arises because of ignorance (*avidyā*). Because there is ignorance, there are volitional formations (*saṃskāra*);

because of volitional formations, there is consciousness (*vijñāna*); because of consciousness, there is name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*); because of name-and-form, there are the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*); because of the six sense bases, there is contact (*sparśa*);

because of contact, there is feeling (*vedanā*); because of feeling, there is craving (*tṛṣṇā*); because of craving, there is grasping (*upādāna*); because of grasping, there is becoming (*bhava*); because of becoming, there is birth (*jāti*).
Birth arises from the causes of birth; old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and affliction all originate with ignorance as their beginning.

Herein, one must directly perceive ignorance, subdue it, and bring it to an end. Once death is ended, one does not die again within death; one cannot deceive others, and all outflows (*āsrava*) are naturally exhausted.
Afflictions are forever severed, the three poisons naturally extinguish themselves, and the roots of evil are spontaneously removed. This requires that one directly cut through the root source.
Do not look back at the branches, tips, flowers, or leaves; if the root is severed, the flowers and leaves will die of themselves.
Sweep away the ground of the mind until its form is no longer seen. When the body is exhausted, ignorance is exhausted;

when the dust and grime are exhausted, the sins accumulated over kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges are all at once suddenly stilled, and one is at once liberated from the cycle of birth and death like a rabbit escaping. But tell me, what is it like?
Ha! The dung beetle leaves its manure ball; shedding the shell, it transforms into a golden cicada. Do you understand?
Within the mind, the nature is unclouded and perfectly luminous; throughout the entire world, all is empty and level as one vast plain.
Not a blade of grass grows, all dust and soil are exhausted; a single orb of the sun rises from within the sea.
Nor is there an exhaustion of ignorance.
Once the eighteen realms (*dhātu*) of the mind-ground have been swept away, the body is necessarily pure; one even forgets that there is such a thing as the "exhaustion of ignorance.
When deluded, it is inverted false thinking, which is the karma of ignorance; when the mind awakens, it transforms the mundane into the sacred.
The Sage and the perfectly luminous awakened nature are one and the same; it is only a matter of whether the mind-ground has been enlightened or remains unenlightened.
The Supreme One said: "They emerge from the same source yet bear different names. Yongjia said: "The true nature of ignorance is itself Buddha-nature;
the illusory and empty body is itself the Dharma-body. If you cling to this illusory body as being 'self,' then there is ignorance, and with ignorance, there is existence and non-existence."
When ignorance arises, the three poisons are produced and the three evil karmas are initiated; these three karmas darken the mind, rendering the six sense faculties internally blind.
Consequently, one fails to see or know, turning away from awakening and uniting with the dust of sensory objects, thereby falling into the three evil realms.

If there is a person of wisdom who can transform a mind of stinginess and greed into a mind of joyful relinquishment, transform a mind of anger and resentment into a mind of joy, and transform a mind of delusion...
Transform the clinging mind into a mind of perfect integration and liberation; transform the six thieves into spiritual powers.
Thus, each and every thing is turned and transformed naturally, converting the mundane into the sacred. The ordinary person is itself the sage;
if one cannot turn and transform them, then the sage is itself the ordinary person. How is it that the common person is turned by external objects?
If a person can transform objects, the common people will use them daily without realizing it;
though they are busy all day long, being led by objects, as days and months pass, they gradually distance themselves from their home and fail to return, losing the truth and forgetting the source.
If one understands that the myriad things return to oneself, how could one ever lose the true source? Master Chuan said: "In the end..."

"Though busy all day with myriad affairs, there is no hindrance; seeking neither liberation nor delighting in heaven, one can, in a single thought, return to non-thought and stride with high steps upon the crown of Vairocana. It is also said:
"All day long eating rice, one never bites a single grain; all day long wearing clothes, one never hangs a single thread. Dao said:
Dwelling in the dust, one is not stained by the dust; existing amidst desire, one is without desire. Body and mind are as one, with nothing remaining within or without.
One must forge them into a single whole, equal in form and shadow to the empty kalpa. When body and shadow no longer exist, the essence is revealed in its majestic dignity.
As soon as there is even a speck of dust, emptiness arises throughout the entire realm, and one immediately falls into birth and death. Simply turn back and contemplate your own body—your very self.
When all else is unreal and empty, even my own body is but a provisional existence—how can ignorance be so profound?
Tell me, how does one lose the true path? *Ei!* Snow obscures the woodcutter’s way; clouds hide the herb-gatherer.
The path ahead is dark and vast; Boundless rivers and ten thousand jagged peaks.
If you possess even a fraction of the power to turn back, The Great Way is majestic, level, and wide— Reaching even unto the end of old age and death.
Once this is attained, there will never again be any further anxiety, suffering, aging, or death. A practitioner must forget their form and forget their body;
since the self-body is non-existent, what ignorance can there be? Since ignorance is non-existent, birth and death are also severed.
The Supreme One said: "Internally observe the mind, yet the mind has no mind; externally observe the form, yet the form has no form. Far...
When one contemplates things, one finds that each thing lacks the nature of a thing; once these three aspects are realized, there is only emptiness perceived.
The *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: "There is no mark of self, no mark of person, no mark of sentient being, and no mark of life-span.

When these three are absent, all four marks are empty. Since what ignorance, old age, and death could there be? All phenomena are naturally empty; this is precisely what constitutes a sage or a Buddha.
Even these two terms, "Immortal" and "Buddha," are superfluous; they are merely forced designations.

Furthermore, sentient beings are inverted, deluded by the illusory phenomena before their eyes, and led astray by habitual tendencies. Their forms and shadows shift and change, yet they cannot act as masters;

they drift along with the flow of things because they cling to a self. As their deluded minds are not extinguished and their notions of self and other are not eliminated, they remain attached to sounds.
Form falls into birth and death; yet for one who has seen their nature, there is no dharma before the eyes, nor are there sentient beings.
Mind, Buddha, and sentient beings are fundamentally without distinction; they are the equal, true Dharma-realm, observed as a single body.
All phenomena return to the One. But tell me, how do they observe them as the same? The Immortal Sage said: "Though the branches may diverge,"
Although there are slight differences until they return to the root in the *Man'yō*, their branching schools and divergent streams ultimately flow back to the sea.

Furthermore, before the Great Ultimate (*taiji*) was divided, all was a single undifferentiated breath; how could there have been duality? Once heaven and earth were separated, there arose high and low;
from one came two, from two came three, and from three came the myriad things—all of which were transformations of that single non-being.
Heaven is the Way, the earth is the Way, and human beings are the Way; all things, whether sentient or insentient, are born from the breath of the Way.
When observing the branches and tips, the myriad species appear unequal; yet when knowing the root, they are all without distinction.
As the Śūramgama Sūtra says: "This Dharma is equal, without high or low. The Immortals and Perfected Ones say: "Equality is non-duality."

An eternal man of true integrity— If one can discern this principle, then birth follows its own course, aging follows its own course, sickness follows its own course, and death follows its own course.
Birth, aging, sickness, and death never obstruct me; bubbles arise and bubbles perish— the surging waves and overflowing waters are ever thus.
Dadian said: "One who has reached the ultimate home perceives neither birth and death nor arising and ceasing;
as for heaven and hell, the six realms, and the four modes of birth—all are illusory transformations that have no connection whatsoever with one who has reached the bottom.
Naturally, such a person lets go of their entire being. An ancient said: "All conditioned phenomena are impermanent; all are empty, and this very emptiness is the Tathāgata."
Great Perfect Enlightenment. Now tell me, when one dies, where does one go? Do you understand?
A single wheel of shadowless sun stands upright within the great void.
Since the delusory manifestations of ignorance have been exhausted through the dissolution of the body, there is nothing more to grasp.
Contemplating emptiness is itself empty; birth and death have no means of approaching it, nor is there an exhaustion of old age and death.
Since there is neither old age nor death, the eternal kalpa remains as such; how could there be any exhaustion? That which has an end is but a phantom realm of form.
The body being without aging or death is the characteristic mark of true emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
Since one neither clings to existence nor stagnates in emptiness, it is lively and agile, rolling and turning, perfectly round and brilliantly radiant—how could there be any end to this?

Furthermore, a practitioner at the beginning of their path must first strike through and clear away [all obstructions) until it is thoroughly purified; only then will there be some point of resonance.
The Most High said: "Diminish it again and diminish it until one reaches non-action;
through non-action, there is nothing that is not done. Da Dian said: "A person who studies the Way is like peeling a plantain tree;
layer after layer is removed until they are exhausted, leaving no place for the hand to grasp. Then, naturally, one returns to the root and source and attains the Five [Fruits]."
The aggregates are empty like that which has not yet arisen; they are as if completely incinerated until one reaches the state where emptiness and non-emptiness are indistinguishable.
There, the entire substance is forgotten and no trace remains. To possess the eyes and hands of the whole body, not even a speck of dust may be established.
Even names cannot be found, let alone anything else—the twelve links of dependent origination, the six perfections, the myriad practices, or the ascetic austerities of *dhūta*—all vanish at once.
Suddenly liberated, like withered wood or dead ashes, such a person is one who has not encountered anything at all.
As the Ancients said: "It is not a matter of stilling the mind to eliminate delusive thoughts; it is simply because there is nothing to be contemplated.
If one further speaks of birth and death, cause and effect, or mind and nature, Yongjia said: "The mind is the root; dharmas are the dust. Two...
The seeds are like stains and grime upon a mirror; only when they are entirely removed does the light finally appear.
When both mind and phenomena are forgotten, one reaches the ground where there is neither birth nor death. But tell me, when both person and dharma are forgotten, what is it that remains?
Do you understand? Ashes fly and smoke vanishes—where is the home? Water is distant, the sky is vast, all one color in autumn.
When both person and phenomena are forgotten, all affairs come to rest; the hundred rivers and four seas converge at their source and flow.
Suddenly, the moon of the vast sky bursts forth, illuminating heaven and earth so that the Four Great Elements are devoid of suffering, accumulation, cessation, and the path.
Once one has forgotten their physical form, birth and death are severed; there is no further exhaustion, and what suffering, accumulation, cessation, or path could there be?
My former teacher said: "Because of having a body and mind, one invites manifold sufferings. If one can forget the substance of the mind, how can suffering arise?
The commentary says: "The body is the root of all suffering; the mind is the root of evil karma. If one can let them go..."
Body and mind will then ascend to the other shore of Bodhi. Great颠 (Dian) said:

"For those of the Lesser Vehicle who practice the six perfections and myriad deeds with diligence day and night, seeking the Dharma outside the mind—there is no such place where they can escape these Four Truths, transcend the Three Realms, or avoid the cycle of rebirth.
The Buddhas appear in the world for the sake of the Great Matter; they do not do so for the sake of the Lesser Vehicle."
The Dharma delivers sentient beings; those of the Mahāyāna study the unconditioned dharma (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*). Sitting upright, they contemplate the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*);
all transgressions are like frost and dew, which the sun of wisdom can eliminate. Dwelling in a secluded place, they collect and restrain their minds, sitting upright and unmoving.
They observe that all phenomena (*dharma*) are non-existent and contemplate that the body composed of the four great elements has no sensation.
The essence is signless, thereby clarifying the truth; one knows for oneself that it is empty and quiescent. Sudden contemplation reveals its purity and exhaustion;
it is the function of non-action that remains unimpaired through long kalpas. It is the practice of non-activity, wherein one does not act; it is suchness, immovable, profoundly and eternally still.
The Lotus Sutra says: "All dharmas are from the very beginning eternally in the state of quiescent extinction.

When the sons of the Buddha have practiced the Way, they shall become Buddhas in future ages. Adorned with the power of concentration and wisdom, there is neither delusion nor enlightenment, neither suffering nor pleasure, neither accumulation nor cessation, neither the Path nor attainment, neither wisdom nor loss;
from the beginning, not a single thing exists—even a bright mirror is likewise so.
If one does not attain realization here at this very platform, there will be no end to defilement, and one cannot leap directly into the stage of the Tathāgata.
Do you wish to see the Tathāgata? The Tathāgata seems to come but does not come; he seems to go but does not go. If you try to send him away, you cannot;
if you try to detain him, he does not stay. Do you understand? Dense bamboo does not hinder the flowing stream.
Passing over the mountain, how could its height obstruct the flight of white clouds?
Without suffering, accumulation, cessation, or the path—how profound! Suddenly and utterly purified, one beholds the Tathāgata.
Fools seek the thirty-two marks externally; I walk with you as a companion, yet you do not recognize me.
There is neither ignorance nor attainment.

Since even one's own body is but a provisional construct, how could there be any attainment? The Master said: "In truth, there is nothing attained; it is only for the sake of transforming sentient beings that we speak of 'attaining the Way.
The Commentary says: "There is neither person nor Buddha; throughout the great trichiliocosm, as vast as the sands of the Ganges, all are within the ocean."
"Blow away all sages and worthies like a flash of lightning. It is also said: "It is not mind, not Buddha, and not things. Dadian said:
"When one reaches such a state, it is like a thief entering an empty room; there is nothing to steal. A sutra says:
"To be free from all extremes is called the wondrous Way. The Master [Shenhui] further said: "The self-nature..."
In purity, there is not a single dharma that can be grasped by the mind; from the beginning, the "Dharma entrusted" has been entrusted as being fundamentally non-existent.
Each person awakens within their own mind; having awakened, there is neither existence nor non-existence. There is no gain and no loss, no progress and no cultivation.
As soon as there is even a hair’s breadth of "gain," "loss," "I am able," "I understand," "I have awakened," or "I have attained" within the breast, [it is already a delusion].
Those who are clever and possess wisdom are all people of overweening pride; if I do not eliminate them, they will all fall into birth and death.
Those who are true seekers of the Way are not like this at all; they naturally possess a path for their own emergence.
But tell me, what is this path of emergence? Strike until the four quarters are pure, And you shall naturally be able to move forward.
Originally, this has not a speck of dust; I only fear that people of the present age mistake it for reality.
When one lets go and realizes there is not a single thing, where would it not be the springtime of Wuling?
It is because there is nothing to be attained.
Attaining non-attainment, the one essence is empty and void. When a practitioner reaches this point, they enter the stage of the Mahāyāna.
Why do sentient beings transmigrate and cannot find rest? It is because they have not yet seen their nature;
lacking wisdom, they cannot extensively awaken to the meaning of immeasurable emptiness. Clinging to their own intellectual understanding within their own chests, they go astray.
The Original Mind: Dadian said, "That which enters from without is not one's own treasure.
Xianzhen said, "To learn the words within another's mind is ultimately the speech of another person. Sentient beings, being possessed by dry wisdom (*śuṣka-prajñā*), study and understand extensively;
these accumulated habits remain in the mind and thus give rise to arrogance (*māna*). An ancient said, "If there is even a hair’s breadth [of attachment], it is dust upon every speck of dust."
If you do not digest this, you will merely know the stories and rumors of phenomena;
if it is digested, all objects are exhausted and you personally see and personally know all things, like a person with clear vision ascending a high mountain and seeing nothing obstructed.

A practitioner must reach the ultimate limit of the empty kalpa, remaining equally beyond falling into secondary views; only by returning to the root and attaining the essential meaning is there true resonance. If one is attached...
Because I harbored contempt for those who clung to the notion of a self, the bhikṣu Śunakṣatra, though he could expound the Vimalakīrti Sūtra, was not rid of his overweening pride and fell into hell.
Because I did not eliminate greed and anger when the Dharma Master Yunguang preached and celestial flowers rained down in profusion, I fell into the Avīci Hell like a tethered ox.
If you wish to transcend the Buddhas and patriarchs, you must practice moment by moment.
The world is empty and still, a phantom transformation; all adventitious defilements are but the substance of the great void.
Sound and form do not exist, not even a speck of dust can be established; it is like space itself. This is the person who has realized the matter—the one of pure clarity and peaceful bliss.
Do you wish to see this person of pure clarity and peaceful bliss? Not a single thread of silk hangs upon them—everywhere they go, they are free.
Since we met, you have been bare-chested with not a thread upon you; walking and sitting together, who knows you?
We only recognize you as Zhang San or Li Si; we do not know what family you belong to.

*Bodhisattva*. "Bodhisattva" is a term from the Sanskrit language of the Western Heavens; in the Eastern Land, it is translated as "emptiness of persons" (*pudgala-śūnyatā*) and "emptiness of phenomena" (*dharma-śūnyatā*).
Dadian said: "To fully realize the emptiness of persons is called *bodhi*; to fully realize the emptiness of phenomena is called *sattva*."
When both person and phenomena are empty, it is called "wondrous enlightenment.

If those of the four fruits of the Small Vehicle practice with attachment to signs, engaging in diligent and ascetic practices, and even reach the cultivation of the out-flow-free path to sever the dust-like delusions—thereby perfecting their fruitive conduct and attaining the fourth fruit of Arhatship—they are like a gazelle leaping alone;
their supernormal powers are narrow and inferior, and they fall into the ranks of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.
If the fruit cannot connect with things to benefit sentient beings, and if one does not see one's nature, one cannot reach the stage of the Perfect and Sudden Teaching.
It is essential to see one's nature; once nature is seen, in the space of a palm-turn, one transforms from an ordinary person into a sage.

Spontaneously, through karmic conditions, one awakens to the Buddha-samādhi and knows the source of the Great Way. This consists solely of the teacherless wisdom and the spontaneous wisdom, which are manifold in their various aspects.
Through skillful means, they deliver all who are deluded, so that both the awakened and the deluded may ascend together to the other shore and never again undergo birth.

This is the separate transmission outside the teachings, requiring no blade of grass; it is entry into the unimpeded Dharma-gate of the Perfect and Sudden. But tell me, what is this unimpeded Dharma-gate?
It is to look back with equanimity upon the one level, where the seven paths and eight crossings are all thoroughly traversed.
When many waters unite, they do not distinguish between clear and turbid; when many fires gather, they shine as one.
The fruit must reach the destination without divergent paths; the broad, level Way is uniformly even.
It is by relying on the Prajñāpāramitā.
These six characters in between are explained according to the preceding *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*: by practicing one attains great wisdom;

having attained wisdom, one necessarily ascends to the other shore. Furthermore, the most honored and supreme awakened nature—*prajñā*—is such that there is nothing in heaven or on earth that can equal it.
The Way says: "A single day of conditioned existence is not as good as a single moment [of the unconditioned]."
Regarding the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*): it is further said that "studying the teachings for one year is not as good as practicing the Way for a single day.

An ancient worthy said, "Studying wisdom (*prajñā*) for a thousand days is not as good as studying *prajñāpāramitā* for a single day. Dadian said, "When *prajñā* is thoroughly penetrating, it is the Great Luminous Treasury;
it is like a person entering the sea—the deeper they enter, the deeper it becomes—thereby opening the Buddha’s knowledge and vision and awakening to the Buddha’s knowledge and vision."

Behold the great supernatural powers and transformations, manifesting through manifold skillful means in various forms to benefit beings according to their capacities, never falling into a second state.
The single essence is observed as the equal, true Dharma-realm; there are no sentient beings to be saved, nor is there any Buddha to be made.
Do you understand? When the waters flow in different streams, they become one when they reach the sea.
Yuan: Hehe! I only fear that it will scatter and disperse beyond recovery—a broken mirror cannot be refitted, and fallen blossoms cannot be returned to the branch.
Once the Prajñāpāramitā is realized, all temperaments and natures are harmonized and return to the One.
Silently penetrating through—what a marvelous return! At midnight, the void is like broad daylight;
the mind is free from obstruction.
By practicing according to this Prajñāpāramitā, one immediately attains a mind free from obstruction and awakens to the Truth.
As the wondrous principle is vast and penetrating, the great void is pure and inherently so, eternally attaining mastery.

The Immortal Master said: "If the mind is like the great void, it is not stained by a single thing. The Buddha said: "The mind is identical to empty space; phenomena are shown to be equal to empty space.
When the realization of emptiness is attained, there is neither 'is' nor 'non-is. Since it is thus merged with empty space...
If they are of one essence, what difference is there between that which is and that which is not? There is external purity, internal purity, and both external and internal purity;
there is external emptiness, internal emptiness, and emptiness as the very substance itself. Before heaven and earth existed, this emptiness already existed.
The Most High said: "There was something formless yet complete, born before heaven and earth. He further said: "Nameless, it is the beginning of heaven and earth;
with name, it is the mother of the myriad things. One gazes at it and does not see it; one listens for it and does not hear it;
one grasps for it and does not find it. Facing it, its head is not seen; following it, its tail is not seen. Even the Five Eyes cannot perceive its traces.
Second, when listening, one hears its resonance. The Old Man of the River said: "The Great Way is majestic and brilliant, clearly manifest;
it is inherently possessed by every person and perfectly realized by each individual. It is only because of a single mistaken thought that the myriad forms appear.
The Sixth Patriarch said: "I have a thing that reaches up to heaven and down to the earth; no one recognizes it—if you see it intimately..."
On one hand, transcending Buddhas and patriarchs, emerging from the triple world, and not falling into saṃsāra;
for oneself, to be willing and to have self-confidence, being able to nurture and preserve the unimpeded Dharma until it is definitively free of obstruction. Do you understand?
Tear apart the net that covers the heavens; cast off the summons from before your face.
Space is difficult for objects to adhere to; what hindrance or obstruction could there be?
Break through the bottom of the wash-tub, and you shall see Avalokiteśvara, free from all obstructions.
The continuous arising of conceptual thoughts is called "attachment"; the failure to turn back from objects is called "obstruction.

To speak again of "non-attachment and non-obstruction" means that both internally and externally one is pure, and all conditions are liberated and carefree. It is like the brilliant sun in a clear sky, its light filling the great trichiliocosm, shining everywhere without exception;
all illusory realms are entirely free from attachment and obstruction, flowing boundlessly to the east and to the west.
Transcending the infinite, moving freely in all directions, it cannot be constrained by illusory phenomena;

this fundamental source-nature is the naturally authentic body that remains unimpaired through long kalpas—without going or coming, without change or difference. Do you wish to see this body unimpaired through long kalpas?
When the mist disperses, the sun first appears; when the dust settles, the mirror naturally shines.
Originally empty and without obstruction, one becomes deluded by clinging to appearances;
if a person can turn back [from this], they will be equal to both immortals and Buddhas.
Thus it is said.
Therefore, the single word "therefore" (*gù*) is the perfection of the ultimate limit; it is also the principle of true permanence (*zhēncháng*), which cannot be expressed in words.
Because it cannot be spoken, it is called "therefore. The *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* says: "There is no dharma that can be preached; this is called preaching the Dharma. The Confucians say:
"The Way is fundamentally without words; when one speaks, the principle of the Way is lost. The Immortal Master said: "The Way is difficult to speak of; it must..."
One must awaken for oneself. But tell me, how does one attain awakening? *Ei!* A single strike of the golden bell resounds, startling the dreamer awake.
Because it is the ultimate state of true permanence and perfection, it is omnipresent and difficult to defile—vividly alive everywhere.
Adapting to circumstances and responding to conditions, there are myriad ways; yet one walks alone in vast openness and carefree ease, without fear.
Since the mind is free from hindrance, the True Constant is spontaneously perfected—what further cause for a fearful heart could there be?
If one reaches this ground and awakens to the emptiness of nature, such that east and west cannot be distinguished and north and south cannot be discerned;

if one is not deceived by light and darkness, not obstructed by corners and walls, not confined by yin and yang, and not enslaved by the forces of creation—then for one like this, what sorrow or suffering is there to fear?
What birth and death is there to dread? One does not [participate] with the myriad...
Taking the Dharma as one’s companion, one should walk alone and stride forth; ascending to heaven, one looks upward without end; entering the earth, one goes downward without limit.
Mountains, rivers, stone walls, and the elements of earth, water, fire, and wind—coming and going through these, there is no obstruction whatsoever.
Walking a thousand *li* with the palm of the hand turned sideways, the return journey is like flying; neither heaven nor earth can restrain such a one, and neither ghosts nor spirits can fathom them.
He is called the Sovereign Great Awakened Golden Immortal. Do you wish to see this Sovereign Golden Immortal?
There is no need to seek torches or lamps; when hungry he eats and when thirsty he drinks, always facing you.
Coming and going with ease and leisure, there is neither fear nor sorrow;
unable to remain within the realm of illusory transformations, one walks alone and strides solitary upon the Isle of the Immortals,
far removed from inverted dreams and delusions.
If one is free from obstructions and devoid of fear, one naturally transcends inverted thoughts and delusive dreams.

The Immortal Master said: "During the day there are no discursive thoughts; at night, dreams are few. The Buddha said: "Dreams arise because of thoughts, and thoughts originate because of mindfulness.
People of the world know only that there are dreams when the eyes are closed, but they do not realize that there are also dreams when the eyes are open. How can this be?"

This is dreaming with eyes open. A former master once said: "Even if gold and silver were to pass as high as the Northern Dipper, when the great limit of one's life arrives, it is all within a single dream.
Is this not dreaming even while one's eyes are open?

If you wish to awaken from the dream, you must wait for impermanence (*anityatā*) before you will finally realize that everything done, everything performed, and everything craved and grasped throughout your life—all these myriad conditions—are entirely nothing but a dream.
This spring dream is merely for one’s own sake and cannot protect one from official duties; by the time one realizes this, it will already be too late.

If there is a person of wisdom who suddenly attains self-reflection and self-awakening that impermanence has arrived, they will realize that all these cravings and attachments are the seeds of saṃsāra and the causes of hell, and will thus distance themselves from delusion and awaken to the truth.
In the emptiness of intrinsic nature, one knows that this self is necessarily non-existent. As the ancients said:
"The Sage has no 'self,' no fixedness, no necessity, no ego, no dependence, no reliance; no obscurity and no brightness; no name and no form; no strength and no weakness;
no defilement and no purity; no cessation and no activity; no passivity and no extinction; no silence and no speech—transcending thought and transcending expression."
"Contemplate that all paths of language are severed and the sphere of mental activity is extinguished. The Most High said: "In truth, there is nothing to be attained;
it is for the sake of transforming sentient beings. The Commentary says: "The mystery of the Way is profound and subtle, and cannot be perceived. Daian said:
"When dead and cremated, there is no hunger, no thirst, no cold, no heat, no arising, no falling, and no sitting."
In sleep there are no six sense organs, no nine apertures, no four hundred and four diseases, and no eighty-four thousand parasites;
there is forever no inverted dreaming or delusion. If one does not awaken in this way, then within the pure realm, a single thought-moment is already eight thousand years in Jambudvīpa.
If you understand it in an instant, it is so; if you do not understand it, it is as though countless kalpas have passed from death to birth.
Life unfolds in a succession of states where one is unaware of sleep, remaining in a long dream without waking; for ten thousand kalpas one is inverted and deluded without end.
Invert after invert, death follows birth, and birth follows death; from dream to dream, and from waking to sleep, one becomes more deluded within delusion, with no time of final resolution.
If there is someone who can strike through to the bottom and pass beyond this, they will forever be free.
Inversions, dreams, and illusions are suddenly cast off. But tell me, once they are suddenly cast off, where do they go?
A swift falcon escapes its cage and soars toward the heavens; let it be as it may, no one can come near it.
No thought by day, no dream by night; not being toyed with by the objects of inverted realms, one breaks through the uppermost barrier with a single punch.
Turning the body upward, one ascends directly to the Primordial Cavern, reaching ultimate *nirvāṇa*.

The seeker should instead turn inward to thoroughly investigate their own body, realizing it is entirely false and illusory; that in a single day of impermanence, it will all be destroyed and decayed, making it difficult to feel attachment.
To reach such a definitive conclusion—what then remains? Originally, these four elements do not exist;
yet because worldly people all cling to having a body, they delude themselves by pursuing external objects, abandoning kin for strangers, and mistaking a thief for their own child. This is false.

Taking the four great elements and the six sense faculties as real, one performs various karmas and undergoes various sufferings, transmigrating through ten thousand kalpas without awakening, without knowledge, and unable to attain liberation. Reflect silently upon this day and night, never departing from mindfulness;
awaken yourself and illuminate yourself, investigating minutely these six faculties and five aggregates from the beginningless eons past.
Fundamentally, there is no self; names and forms are all unattainable.

There is neither the realization of immortality nor the attainment of Buddhahood, nor are the six realms and four modes of birth—none of these various things can be found. "Old" means exhaustion. Reaching this point, everything is leveled in universal equality;
it is turned over from the very bottom, all conditions suddenly cease, and nothing remains outside of this. Master Chuanshan said: "It is like cutting [a tree]."
A single handful of silk—cut once, it all breaks at once. It is also said: "With one punch, break through the barrier of the *pura*;
with one kick, overturn the blockage of the Mysterious and Wondrous. Go and come as you please in the north, south, east, and west; do not seek Mahākāruṇika Avalokiteśvara. Dadian said:
"Depart from the four propositions and cut off the hundred negations; when knowledge and views are no longer seen, this is reaching Nirvāṇa."
Furthermore, Nirvana is neither birth nor death; it is precisely what is meant by quiescent extinction, being without birth and without death.
The Great Sage said, "It is profoundly still and eternally tranquil. The Buddhist sutras say, "When birth and death have ceased, quiescent extinction is bliss.
"Quiescent" means still and unmoving; "extinction" means that all phenomena do not arise. In reality, there is no birth and death.
Now tell me, what is the appearance of that which is neither born nor dies? *Pah!* Do not listen to sounds;
they are not the true form. If you recognize emptiness, it is just like this.
In the ultimate sense, one's own body is fundamentally non-existent; You must let go immediately—do not be deluded!
On the path to Nirvana there are no companions; on the Great Way there is no self or person—who is it?
The Buddhas of the three periods of time—Great颠 (Dian) said:
"In the past Adornment Kalpa, there were one thousand Buddhas; in the future Constellation Kalpa, there will be one thousand Buddhas."
In the present Bhadrakalpa there are one thousand Buddhas, and throughout the three periods of time there are three thousand Buddhas;

furthermore, there are Buddhas of the kalpas yet to come, numbering in unspeakably unspeakable quantities that can never be exhausted—all these Buddhas are obtained through cultivation and realization.
The Old Man of Chuanshu said: "Plant melons and you shall reap melons; plant fruits and you shall reap fruits. He also said:

"One Buddha, two Buddhas, ten thousand, a hundred thousand Buddhas—each with eyes askance and noses straight. Because they planted roots of goodness in years past, today they receive their power as before.
The *Scripture of the Way* says: "Plant orchids and you shall obtain fragrance; plant millet and you shall obtain grain. By doing good, blessings descend."
Xiang commits evil and brings down calamity. Furthermore, the Buddhas of the three periods do not attain the human body without cultivation;
yet within this very body, there are likewise such transformations of the Buddhas, which vary according to causes.

Obscured by habitual tendencies and obstructed by objective phenomena, one becomes deluded within oneself and fails to recognize them. If one is without mind regarding the mind, that is the stillness of the Buddhas of the past.
However, immovability is precisely the Buddha of the Future; responding to things without obscuration according to their capacities is precisely the Buddha of the Present;
being pure and untainted is precisely the Stainless Buddha; entering and exiting without hindrance is precisely the Buddha of Spiritual Powers;
roaming freely wherever one goes is precisely the Buddha of Sovereignty; and the non-obscuration of the single mind is precisely the Path of the Radiant Buddha.

When mindfulness is firm, it is precisely the indestructible Buddha. Although each and every Buddha possesses his own body and speaks from it, even their combined explanations could not exhaustively describe its manifestations, which appear in manifold ways yet are but the single Reality.

Simply go and sit in stillness and observe that the past, present, and future are all of one essence, like empty space—without differing characteristics, without self-characteristics, and without other-characteristics. It is non-existent.
The signless is not the grasping of signs; it is neither this shore, nor the other shore, nor the middle stream. Contemplate its quiescence, which is forever uninterrupted and unceasing.
If a person suddenly awakens to this and directly accepts it, then the vast and distant kalpas of emptiness are entirely present right now.
Radiance is emitted and the earth shakes as both person and dharma are forgotten; one no longer perceives the past, future, or present.
To reach the ultimate state of exhaustion and non-exhaustion is precisely the emptiness of emptiness (*śūnyatā-śūnyatā*). Herein, neither self nor non-self can be apprehended;

even "self" and "self" are unattainable. Emptiness and form are likewise non-existent; the three periods of time are empty of themselves, not because consciousness is extinguished, but because the nature of consciousness is itself empty.
The past, future, and present are also empty, yet one does not fall into the view of emptiness. Do you wish to see the Buddhas of the three periods?
Ho! Do not suffer from thirst along the river; do not say you are hungry while holding a cake.
Past, future, and present are all close at hand within the human body, yet people themselves remain oblivious.
Amidst the myriad transformations, few understand them; all things blend together with empty space into a single mass.
By relying on the Prajñāpāramitā,
practitioners must employ a hundredfold skillful means of wisdom to harmonize the habitual tendencies accumulated since beginningless kalpas,
thereby unifying them into the nature of the One True Reality and ascending to the other shore; if one does not perceive this nature, it will be extremely difficult to achieve success.

This phrase is the mother of all Buddhas of the three periods of time; the Buddhas of the ten directions rely upon it for their practice, and when their fruit and conduct are perfected, they attain Equal and Perfect Enlightenment.
If one practices apart from this phrase, even if one passes through many kalpas and maintains diligent austerity, those who hope to achieve the Great Way will be few indeed;
such persons belong to the Hinayana teachings and fall into the ranks of the Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, or Arhats.
Whether one be a Buddha, a ghost, a seer, a celestial seer, or an earth seer, the conditioned dharmas will never bring about the attainment of any holy fruit.
One must apply oneself with diligence; by relying upon the Prajñāpāramitā dharma, one attains the Unsurpassed, Right, and True Way.
This alone is the singular path; if one practices otherwise apart from this dharma, it is impossible to succeed.
Abiding herein is the separate transmission outside the teachings; this Dharma is transmitted only after one has personally realized one's own nature.

It is not transmitted by the thousand sages, but through self-awakening and self-confidence. There is no room for the bestowal of predictions regarding the stage of the Perfect and Sudden. Standing alone and marking out the Dharma, one seeks a good spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) and questions the ultimate person.
Relying on the teacher’s instruction, one attains awakening through affinity. The Perfect and Sudden teaching has thus reached its culmination.
If human nature possesses a private mind in the transmission [of the Dharma], this is the teaching of external paths. Where there is entrustment, there is transmission;
where there is gain, there is loss; where there is instruction and bestowal—all these are the false views of external paths, the very root of birth and death.
The Immortal Master said: "There are three thousand six hundred gates of Dharma; this path of cultivation is the true one.
One must know that there is a profound mystery which does not reside within these three thousand six hundred gates. The Immortal Buddhas and Patriarchs cultivated and realized it for themselves;
they originally had no words or phrases, nor did they bestow a single Dharma upon others. If there were a single Dharma to be transmitted as a prediction, [it would not be the truth]."
He is named Śākyamuni, yet he is not called a "Way-man. The Way is fundamentally wordless; it merely teaches people to cultivate themselves and awaken on their own.
To speak of it is not true; one must transcend [reliance on others] and see for oneself. When seeing, there is nothing to be seen.
If you are corrupted by the teachings of others, you must urgently spit it out. Generally, when acting for others, you must let the priceless jewel flow forth from yourself, using it without end.
Those of the highest capacity awaken to a thousand truths upon hearing it once and possess the great *dhāraṇī*;

those of middling and lower capacities hear much yet mostly lack faith. The Great Sage said: "The superior man, hearing the Way, practices it with diligence; the middling man, hearing the Way, is as if it exists and as if it does not;
the inferior man, hearing the Way, laughs at it. This is indeed a teaching difficult to believe, for it is rare.
Do you understand this matter? The people of the world only know how to follow after shadows; they do not know how to leave the shadow and return home.
*Sha!* Cast off your garments and see your true form; when not a single thread remains, you attain peace and security.
If a person wishes to transcend the shadow of their own body, they shall attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* by walking beneath a tree that has no branches.
This is a term from the Sanskrit of the Western Heavens: *anu* means "no," *tara* means "above," and *samyak* means "right."
The term *sambodhi* (三菩提) is translated in the Eastern Land as "True and Perfect" (正真). It is also said to mean "Attaining Equal and Perfect Enlightenment" (成等正覺).
These four characters must be personally realized. As the ancients said: "Only upon seeing the Way does one cultivate it; if one has not seen it, what is there to cultivate?
Though the entire Tripitaka speaks of these four characters, it cannot exhaustively describe them; even the Buddhas could not fully explain them.
The sages and worthies of the three teachings all cultivated these four characters, thereby fully returning to the holy path and attaining equal and perfect enlightenment.
If people of today can practice according to this Dharma of Prajñāpāramitā and Samyaksaṃbodhi, they will attain vast and sudden awakening,
personally behold the Unsurpassed Right Truth, and know for themselves that they shall directly transcend to the rank of Immortal or Buddha in the future.
If you wish to see the unsurpassed, true, and correct [enlightenment], it is manifest in every place and complete in every thing.
The wondrous Way and empty space are its progenitors; its clear manifestations differ from one another.
If a person awakens to the Way of True Permanence, they will recognize their original lord from of old.
Therefore, one knows that the *prajñāpāramitā* is the divine power by which,
through cultivation, one attains the vision of the unsurpassed, right, and true path;
and it is by means of the hundredfold wisdoms of the compassionate Buddhas of the past who pity all sentient beings [that this is known].
By the power of expedient means, he follows along with sentient beings to benefit them and guide those who come after;
he manifests images and transformed persons, employs clay sculptures and wood carvings, and utilizes yellow scrolls and red axes to explain causes and effects.

He uses these provisional names to lead sentient beings, employing the matters of karmic retribution for good and evil and the discourse on heavens and hells to cause people to reform their wickedness and turn toward goodness, thereby departing from the provisional.
This is the sequential guidance through the stages of the ten sages and three worthies of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas who have returned to the truth, as well as the stages of all Buddhas.
The Immortal Master said: "A journey of a thousand *li* is advanced step by step. The Commentary says:
"A jeweled terrace eight thousand fathoms high is not ascended in a single leap. Suddenly, through self-awakening and seeing one's own nature, one transcends the ranks of all Buddhas.
To leap directly into the stage of the Tathāgata: if you do not see your nature, seeking outwardly will never lead to accomplishment.
Awakening has its years, months, days, and times. As the ancients said: "In studying the Way, one must first have an awakening;
if there is no awakening, then whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, one must urgently save oneself outside of words and letters—this is identical to sudden awakening."
The Master said: "Though one may study the Way for a thousand days, awakening occurs in a single moment. It is precisely in this single moment that one attains lightness and ease;
all those of superior virtue return to the same place. If you rely on intellectual understanding, you are merely the spittle of the ancients—nothing but heterodox views and delusions.
You will follow the various paths of birth and death, receiving retribution according to your karma, and cannot even be spoken to. Have you not heard?"
Subhūti had practiced for aeons as numerous as motes of dust before finally attaining the foremost understanding of emptiness beneath the assembly of Śākyamuni.
During the Vaipulya assembly, when Vajrapāṇi questioned him regarding the four-line verse, he attained sudden and total enlightenment. Weeping and wailing, he lamented:
"The wisdom-eye I previously attained was not yet aware of this sutra; all Buddhas of the three periods of time have emerged from it."
The Sūtra flows forth: What is this sūtra? When viewed, there is not a single character; Right where it is, it radiates light.
Without relying on wisdom, one cannot cross the deep river; For ten thousand kalpas, one will sink and drown in the waves.
Having already reached the other shore and returned to the True Way, what need is there to further recite "Svāhā"?
This is the Great Divine Mantra.
If one realizes *pāramitā*, one then beholds this Great Divine Mantra; this divine mantra is possessed by every person.
Not cultivating and not seeing is also the Dharma-gate of the sentient beings' mind-ground, which possesses great spiritual power.
The Daoists say: "When the mind has a sovereign master, the myriad evils cannot invade. The Confucians say: "When the mind is upright, one can ward off evil.
The *Duren Jing* says: "The myriad evils do not disturb him, for the divine spirits guard his door. It is able to expel the heterodox, establish the orthodox, and transform death.
When a person practices to bring others to life, they transform demonic realms into celestial paradises; every manifestation appears, and every object is fully revealed.
Picking things up with one’s own hand, there is nothing that does not accord with ease. This Great Divine Mantra—when the mind stirs or a thought arises, ghosts and spirits are extinguished;
returning to the root and source, externalists’ souls are struck with terror and their spirits submit in submission. This is the Secret Mantra. Recognize this!
Jumma! His supernormal powers and wondrous functions—where do they not accompany him?
Possessing great majestic spiritual power, he subdues the demonic with a single stroke of his sword;
where do they not accompany him? Those living together with him do not recognize it.
This is a great vidyā-mantra.
Possessing great majestic spiritual power, a single point of numinous light naturally radiates and shines forth, penetrating and illuminating the ten directions;
it pierces through the three realms, mountains, rivers, and the great earth without any obstruction, surpassing the sun and moon in its reach, leaving no place unilluminated.
The Ancestor Lü said: "A single point of the mind-lamp flares up in flame; no need for laborious trimming, it shines forth with brilliant clarity.
When attained, it pierces through the darkness of the human world, radiating alone a cold light that fills the Great Void. Although he has thus explained it, one still does not understand it oneself.
If you wish to understand, wipe away the dust from the mirror, and you will see your original nature.
The face:
its brilliant radiance fills the great thousandfold world-system. Fools do not see it, being dragged by their emotions;
If one can let go, there is nothing at all— As before, the mind-nature and the celestial moon are full.
This is the unsurpassed mantra.
By it, one attains the vision of one's own radiance, which illuminates all previous darkness such that nothing can surpass it;
this divine mantra is supreme and none exceeds it. This is the foremost, for all dharmas do not transcend it.
The mind-mantra is the unsurpassed mantra. The Daoists say that the mind is the sovereign of the multitude; the Buddhists say that the mind is the king among dharmas.
For this reason, it is unsurpassed. It is but a single thing: when the King does not move, the myriad subjects naturally find peace;
when the mind is not disturbed, all deviant influences do not arise. Do you understand?
The heart-mantra is supreme; when one goes to a secluded place for contemplation and neither person nor ox is seen, that is the Vulture Peak,
eternally the peerless mantra.
This divine mantra has no equal; it is ineffable and incomparable, without limit or boundary.
This mantra is rarely spoken of in the world, and it is difficult to believe; one must personally encounter this mantra. Do you wish to see this mantra?
When unfolded, it is the vast empty space; when gathered back, not even a hair’s breadth of a thing can be established.
Originally there are no equal things; the divine nature alone is most honored. Heaven and earth can hardly cover and sustain it;
it abides forever, eternally present, able to eliminate all suffering.
If one attains the vision of one's true nature, there will be no further suffering or calamity.

The Buddha’s intention is one of compassion, pitying sentient beings who fall into the mundane world and wander through kalpas, undergoing endless suffering without being able to return to their original source.

Therefore, he manifests various forms appearing in the world and establishes diverse skillful means to rescue and deliver the deluded masses, so that they may all emerge together from the burning house.
Those who possess wisdom should listen attentively to the words of the Great Way and investigate only the ground of the mind, seeking nothing elsewhere.
First, one must sweep it clean, removing the habitual tendencies accumulated over kalpas. Dadian said: "When you dig a pond, you do not wait for the moon;
once the pond is complete, the moon comes of its own accord. For a practitioner, the mind-ground must first be pure, and then [enlightenment] will naturally arise.
Regarding the Way: Confucianism says to regulate the mind through ritual; Buddhism says to gather and collect the mind while dwelling in seclusion;
and Daoism says to subdue the mind and sever all thoughts. The sages of these three teachings teach only that sentient beings must make their minds tranquil, pure, and empty.
If the mind is free from defilement, one naturally perceives one's nature. Once this nature is perceived, one will forever escape the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*) and no longer...
Having attained the Way of neither death nor birth, and having followed the various Buddhas and sages of antiquity through long periods of arduous practice, one finally realizes one's nature;
every thought and every moment encounters the source everywhere. But tell me, where does one go at the very end?
If you do not realize it, you are lost everywhere on the way home; once you have awakened, you are always in your own native land.
For what reason do immortals and Buddhas appear in the world? It is solely because of their compassionate pity for the multitudes sinking in the mire.
If a person is willing to step onto the bow of the boat, they will avoid being a person who drags through mud and water.
This is true and not false.

This is the true Dharma discourse, not words of empty flourish; all Buddhas have spoken this divine mantra to deliver sentient beings—it is not a divergent teaching, nor is it a mere polite expression.
Yongjia said: "When realizing the true mark, there is no person and no dharma;
in a single instant, the karma of Avīci is extinguished. All that has marks is entirely false and illusory; only..."
This mark of no-mark is the true mark; though the great trichiliocosm should all perish, this mark does not perish.
Why does it not perish? The Way says: "That which has form is ultimately false; the markless is the true person. It also says:
"The hundred members may all dissolve away, but one thing remains eternally numinous. A Daoist scripture says: "The Primordial Beginning suspended one..."
The precious jewel is within the profound void. A Buddhist sutra says: "I have a priceless jewel tied inside my garment;
though I have sought it day and night, I suddenly see the Muni-jewel. It also says:
"People do not recognize the Muni-jewel, yet they have personally received it within the Tathāgatagarbha. Although this is so, while seeing the Way may be easy, guarding it is difficult.
The Way is difficult. Do you wish to see this pearl? It is perfectly round, its light flashing and brilliant;
it rolls and turns, lively and agile. I always say: it cannot be placed in a coffin (pronounced *guǎn*, rhyme with *yuàn*).
The true luminosity, the priceless jewel, is without distinction within the portion of every person;
it is only because of a slight point of confusion that clouds arise in the blue sky and the moonlight vanishes.
Therefore, I shall now recite the Prajñāpāramitā mantra.
By practicing until this point is reached, one comes to know that the merit of the Prajñā dhāraṇī is supreme;
this phrase concludes the various preceding skillful means, synthesizing them all into one—the Dharma of the Great Total-Holding (Mahādhāraṇī) which returns all to the single mind.

As the ancients said: "One should contemplate the nature of the Dharma-realm; all things are created by the mind alone. And as the Immortals and Sages said: "Good and evil, existence and non-existence [are but the mind]."
All is within the mind. Great Zhen said: "To the deluded, it is the ālayavijñāna that becomes a venomous serpent after death;
to the awakened, it is a secret mantra that attains the dharma of non-arising. The Tathāgata has esoteric words, which Kāśyapa did not conceal.
If a person single-mindedly receives and maintains this divine mantra, their practice will reach fulfillment; one should constantly hold this mantra."
The ghosts and spirits depart, and the various devas listen in silence, ever joyful.
Do you understand this principle? It is not a matter of mere verbal recitation; it requires that the mind uphold it. Open your eyes wide and do not let it slip away!
If you wish to see this mantra, it is not outside, not inside, nor in between, nor both inside and outside. Furthermore—
Where does the Way reside? Do you understand? It is not apart from this very place; do not allow yourself to become deluded.
The ocean of nature is vast and deep, yet it fears the rising of wind. As soon as the wind arises, the waves overturn the sky.
Once the wind subsides and the billows are stilled, a single moon is reflected in the crystal palace.
He then spoke the mantra, saying:
"Recite these four lines of verse to protect those who uphold this sutra, never departing from their side.

Whether recited in forward or reverse order, there is nothing among all worldly aspirations that will not be fulfilled. One must not forget them throughout the twelve periods of the day. — Chapter [Number]
Mo! Do not mistake it.
The myriad sages and thousand worthies reside within your own body; do not allow yourself to obscure the original truth.
For what reason do I urge you so earnestly and raise it up again and again? Each time it is brought forth, it is ever new.
*Gati gati gati*: "Gati" means emptiness of persons; again, "gati" means emptiness of dharmas. When both persons and dharmas are empty, the two types of emptiness are completely forgotten.
Dongxuan said: "After the unmoving state of one's own mind, there further arises the infinite true mechanism. — Dongxian (Cave Immortal)
It is said: "Man and ox are not seen; their traces are utterly lost. The moonlight’s radiance encompasses the ten thousand phenomena within emptiness.
Now, "emptiness of man" merely teaches one to forget form and forget the physical body; "emptiness of dharmas" merely teaches one to forget emotions and sever thoughts.
When all phenomena are discarded and good and evil are merged, one does not cling to one's own self and does not attach to appearances. Suddenly—
Externally one does not know there is a self-body; internally one does not examine whether there is a self-mind; far off one does not know there are various objects.
Upon reaching this point, when everything is completely forgotten, one naturally perceives a message. Yet to speak of a "message" is already to cling to a phenomenon.
Dadian said: "There is no need to hang up an ancient mirror; when day breaks, all is clear. And so it is.
How is the Way? It is the break of dawn; After the golden rooster has crowed three times, A single red orb emerges from the embrace of the sky.
When both person and dharma are forgotten, all affairs come to rest; The incense burner is without fire, cold and whistling.
A single cry of a wild goose beyond the distant heavens— Far waters and the long sky are one color in autumn.
"Pāragate pāragate" means to arrive at emptiness where there is nothing empty. Master Xian said: "Since there is nothing empty, it is thoroughly pure.
Chan Master Huyan said: "Not even recognizing emptiness—how could one cling to that which is empty? If...
Since there is nothing to be emptied, one reaches the other shore; yet even that other shore must be left behind to advance further.
Thus, one will never again undergo birth, the cycle of saṃsāra is severed, birth and death are ended, and all is stilled.
But tell me, what is this state of no-birth and no-death? Do you recognize it? Do not fall asleep! Heh! It is he too.
It turns; you also turn. Facing it directly, one cannot find it. If you wish to see it, wait until it becomes a solid mass.
When emptiness and that which is empty are utterly eliminated, return with ease to accord with the pure void.
Do not refine into stubborn emptiness; do not lose the source. Spontaneously embody the Way and accord with True Suchness (*tathatā*).
"Pāra-saṃgate pāra-saṃgate" is the pure realm of all Buddhas, untainted by the defilements of the five desires.

They cannot be defiled, for like sages and Buddhas who compassionately respond to the capacities of sentient beings to deliver the deluded masses, they move among those of different species, mingling with dragons and snakes where ordinary and holy dwell together. Whether acting in opposition or in accord, their ways are unfathomable even to sages and worthies.
Like the moon reflected in water, appearing in a thousand rivers, yet that true moon remains fundamentally in the sky.
It cannot be grasped or seized, nor can it be defiled. Can it ever be grasped?
Though you may see it intimately, it is difficult to seize; unless one’s body dwells within the great void.
The pure realm transcends conceptual thought; Untainted by even a speck of dust, this is the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa).
Observe the moon of the fifteenth day at the third watch: Its reflection appears in a thousand rivers without any hindrance—bodhi svāhā!

Dadian said: "Bodhicitta is the beginning; *svāhā* is the end. Furthermore, when practicing to enter the Way, one must first give rise to the bodhicitta and apply oneself with courageous diligence, practicing the Path day and night. As the ancients said:

"If the thought of the Path can compete with worldly discursive thoughts, one would have already become an immortal or attained Buddhahood long ago; it is simply that students are unwilling to do so."

If you go straight ahead, you will arrive; because of having three minds and two intentions, you cannot reach the goal. The Immortal Master said: "To count another's mile-stones (the character *hòu* is pronounced *hòu*;
a *hòu* is a boundary marker every five *lǐ*) while not walking yourself, and reciting 'long peace' with your mouth while your mind does not penetrate it, is futile.

If one is a person of true resolve, they cut through things with a single stroke to practice the Way and study the Buddha-dharma, never again regressing or wavering. Furthermore, one must maintain this steadfastly.
Suddenly awakening to the Way and realizing that the fundamental nature is empty, one immediately attains Bodhi, transcends the three realms, and realizes there is nothing to realize;
having attained non-attainment, one becomes vast and pure, arriving at the place of ultimate bliss where resources are inexhaustible.
Therefore, it is said: *Svāhā*. Now tell me, what state must one reach for this to be the point of total penetration?
Where the waters end and the mountains reach their limit, where not even an inch of grass grows—have you reflected on this?
First, give rise to a single heart of Bodhicitta; next, teach that the myriad anxieties shall not invade one another.
Directly cause them to penetrate the very marrow of empty space, and pull out the acupuncture needle used to treat ailments from of old.
The commentary on the sutra is now complete; I leave behind one final piece for my fellow students of later generations to examine and investigate in detail.
Twenty years hence, there shall be a path for you to emerge upon—do not forget this, Old He.
As for those who have reached the other shore, the high masters, they are not subject to this limit.
The Dharma fundamentally arises from the mind, And likewise ceases within the mind.
Since both arising and ceasing depend entirely upon you, I ask that you discern this for yourself. If all is but one’s own mind, What need is there for another’s words?
You must take up the task yourself, Squeeze the iron ox until its blood flows, And pass the tethering rope through its nostrils at dusk.
Firmly grasping the void to form a knot, Tightly bound upon the pillar of non-action.
Do not allow others to be deluded; do not mistake the thief for your son. When the mind and its phenomena are both forgotten, they are utterly severed.
Cease allowing him to deceive you; strike him through with a single blow first. Contemplating the mind, there is no mind; Contemplating phenomena, phenomena also cease.
When neither person nor ox is seen, The azure sky is clear and pristine; Like the full autumn moon, they cannot be distinguished from one another.
The Heart Sutra of the Perfection of Wisdom (End).

The *Prajñāpāramitā-hṛdaya-sūtra* is the very heart of all Buddhas and the vital pulse of all sages. For this reason, since the Tang dynasty, there have been many commentaries among the Buddhist community.
Recently, I obtained a single copy annotated by the layman Zhang Jiu Cheng, known as Wugou (The Undefiled).
In this work, both Chan and teaching are presented together, and both the internal and external aspects are clarified; it is truly a bright lamp in the dark night and a clear light amidst the mist.
I have had this "Hainan Needle" re-engraved and commissioned artisans to embroider it upon woodblocks, desiring to propagate its transmission.
Is this not indeed the sublime wealth of the Buddha-dharma, the wondrous point where form and emptiness coincide?
Written on a winter day in the second year of Jōei (the Year of the Earth-Sheep), at the Mōan Hermitage on Mount Enpū in Tōzan.
